chunks.content: Drugs and Lactation Database (LactMed®) Bethesda (MD): National Institute of Child Health and Human Development ; 2006 -. Copyright and Permissions Attribution Statement: LactMed is a registered trademark of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. The LactMed® database contains information on drugs and other chemicals to which breastfeeding mothers may be exposed. It includes information on the levels of such substances in breast milk and infant blood, and the possible adverse effects in the nursing infant. Suggested therapeutic alternatives to those drugs are provided, where appropriate. All data are derived from the scientific literature and fully referenced. A peer review panel reviews the data to assure scientific validity and currency. Introduction Breastfeeding is one of the most effective practices for promoting child health and survival. The World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) guidelines advise initiating breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, followed by exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months [ ] while continued breastfeeding with complementary foods is recommended for up to two years and beyond [ ]. In Uganda, exclusive breastfeeding rates for the first 6 months range from 40 to 67%, although they vary by region [ – ]. However, as breastfeeding mothers frequently encounter health problems that may necessitate medication, such as postpartum pain, infections, and chronic conditions, they must make informed decisions about safe medication use to avoid potential adverse effects on their infants. Various factors, including healthcare access, education, cultural beliefs, and individual health status, can affect mothers’ medication choices. Medicine use can substantially influence breastfeeding patterns and duration [ ], as certain drugs may interfere with milk production, composition, or flow. Specifically, drugs such as diphenhydramine, pseudoephedrine, haloperidol, and furosemide have been shown to impact milk synthesis and secretion, potentially leading to reduced breastfeeding efficacy or, in some cases, cessation of breastfeeding [ ]. Moreover, there exists a substantial gap in the literature concerning the safety of drugs used during lactation [ ]. While some medications are considered compatible with breastfeeding, limited evidence is available to assess the risks associated with many commonly used drugs. In Uganda, medications that typically require a prescription in many parts of the world, such as antibiotics, diazepam, amitriptyline, and codeine, can be purchased over the counter. This practice may pose potential risks, including improper use, lack of professional guidance, and increased likelihood of adverse effects or antimicrobial resistance [ ]. Similarly, breastfeeding women may resort to self-medication practices, obtaining medications without prescriptions or professional guidance, despite the increasing awareness of the benefits of breastfeeding. Breastfeeding in the context of Human Immunodeficiency Virus/Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (HIV/AIDS) presents additional difficulties. Uganda has made significant progress in the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. National guidelines recommend that women living with HIV and on antiretroviral therapy (ART) exclusively breastfeed for the first six months, followed by continued breastfeeding with complementary feeding for at least 12 months, provided the mother remains adherent to ART. According to the 2023 Uganda Population-Based HIV Impact Assessment (UPHIA), the national HIV prevalence among pregnant and breastfeeding women was estimated at 7.0% [ , ]. ART adherence is critical during breastfeeding to reduce vertical transmission, and concerns about medicine compatibility with breastfeeding may influence medication adherence behaviors among women living with HIV. The topic of safe medication use among breastfeeding women remains under-researched, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) like Uganda. Studies in other populations have shown that commonly used medications among breastfeeding women include analgesics, antibiotics, and antipyretics, regarded as generally safe due to their low levels of transfer to breast milk and low percentage of the dose prescribed to the mother that is received by the infant known as the Relative Infant Doses (RIDs) [ , ]. The RID is calculated as the dose received by the infant through breast milk (mg/kg/day) divided by the maternal dose (mg/kg/day) and expressed as a percentage. A commonly accepted threshold is that a RID of less than 10% is generally considered safe for breastfeeding. In this study, safety classification was based on established international references, including the WHO guidelines, LactMed database, and peer-reviewed pharmacokinetic literature. This approach enables evidence-based categorization of commonly used drugs as compatible, use with caution, or not recommended during breastfeeding. Studies have highlighted that self-medication practices are prevalent among breastfeeding mothers, especially in settings with limited access to healthcare, where women may obtain medications informally without prescriptions. In these settings, many medications requiring a prescription are available over the counter [ , ]. This study contributes to the existing body of evidence by offering specific understandings into medicine use during breastfeeding in Uganda, an area with limited research despite high breastfeeding rates and widespread access to over-the-counter medications. Unlike previous studies that have largely drawn from high-income countries. In particular, the study builds upon recent WHO and UNICEF guidance on breastfeeding by exploring how medication practices influence adherence to exclusive breastfeeding recommendations and duration. Likewise, by identifying commonly used drugs and evaluating their safety profiles, especially in a setting where prescription-only medicines are readily available over the counter, this study generates evidence critical for informing local health policy, clinical decision-making, and public health interventions tailored to breastfeeding mothers in Uganda and comparable LMIC settings. Given these considerations, the study aimed to investigate the prevalence of medicine use, evidence about safety, and factors that influence medicine use among breastfeeding women. Materials and methods Study design and setting This was a cross-sectional study conducted among breastfeeding women attending selected urban healthcare clinics in Kampala, Uganda. The study population included breastfeeding women aged 18 years and older, regardless of HIV status, to capture a comprehensive picture of medication use in this group. Data were collected from six healthcare clinics in Kampala, including the Infectious Diseases Institute (IDI) and Kampala City Council Authority (KCCA) affiliated clinics. These facilities provide a range of free maternal and child health services such as immunization, outpatient and inpatient care, and specialized treatment for people living with HIV. The IDI, a research institution linked to Makerere University’s College of Health Sciences, supports over 200,000 individuals living with HIV through its Health Systems Strengthening Programme. The KCCA clinics serve a diverse urban population of more than half a million people, offering comprehensive healthcare services including maternal and child health (MCH), infant immunizations, growth monitoring, family planning, and general health check-ups. Additionally, these clinics provide health education and counseling, which create opportunities to engage mothers on breastfeeding practices and medication use. Recruiting participants from these sites enabled access to a representative sample of breastfeeding women actively utilizing child health services in urban Kampala. Patient and public involvement The questionnaires were designed and piloted by the investigators and subsequently subjected to user testing by peer mothers affiliated with sexual and reproductive health clinics. This testing aimed to assess the questionnaires’ content, length, and usability, specifically among breastfeeding women. Peer mothers provided crucial feedback during this process, which informed multiple revisions of the questionnaires to enhance clarity and relevance. Beyond the piloting phase, peer mothers played vital roles in providing emotional support, educating breastfeeding women about medication safety, facilitating study participation, promoting adherence to study protocols, and fostering community engagement. Regular meetings with Community Advisory Board (CAB) members and peer mothers were held throughout the study to monitor progress and gather ongoing feedback, strengthening the collaboration between researchers and the community. The involvement of community members, peer mothers, and the CAB has been shown to effectively bridge gaps between researchers and the community, ensuring that study activities remain responsive to community needs [ , ]. These sessions provided a platform for feedback on study implementation. The questionnaires were also reviewed by the authors (LA, CW, RK), and multiple revisions were made to integrate user feedback. Eligibility and recruitment Breastfeeding women aged 18 years and above, irrespective of HIV status, with infants aged 12 months or younger, were included in the study. The women were recruited from MCH clinics located within six urban healthcare facilities across the selected study sites. This infant age range was selected because infants in this stage rely heavily on breast milk for nutrition, and maternal medication use could pose a higher risk of transfer through breast milk. Participants were recruited between September 2023 and January 2024 using systematic random sampling. Based on average clinic attendance, every 5th eligible woman was approached for participation. A total of 294 participants were recruited across six health facilities, with approximately 30 to 31 participants enrolled per site. Since all participating sites had comparable patient volumes, an equal allocation strategy was applied to ensure uniform representation from each facility. The first participant was randomly selected using a lottery method to ensure fairness and reduce selection bias. A total sample size of 294 participants was determined based on the assumption that 80% of breastfeeding women use medicines, a 95% confidence level, a 5% margin of error, and a design effect of 1.0, considering the use of systematic random sampling [ ]. The sample size was calculated using the formula for estimating a single population proportion: n = Z 2 ×p× (1-p)/d 2 . Where: n = required sample size, Z = Z-score corresponding to the desired confidence level (1.96 for 95%), p = estimated prevalence of medication use among breastfeeding women (assumed 80% or 0.8), d = margin of error (set at 0.05). An additional 5% was added to account for potential non-response or incomplete data. These parameters were chosen to ensure adequate precision in estimating the prevalence of medicine use and sufficient power to detect statistically significant associations in the analysis. Data collection procedures The survey questionnaire was developed based on insights from a comprehensive literature review and previously published surveys (1, 2). It was administered face-to-face to potential participants, and a series of structured questions was designed to be completed within 40 min. The questionnaire was professionally translated into Luganda, the most commonly spoken language in the selected study sites. Research assistants were trained to administer the questionnaire. The questionnaire gathered information on demographic characteristics (e.g., maternal age, education level, parity, and child’s age), types of medicines used, and breastfeeding practices. HIV status was self-reported by participants and, where possible, verified using clinic records. No additional HIV testing was conducted during the study, as all participants were recruited from healthcare facilities where HIV testing is routinely provided as part of maternal-child health services. To minimize recall bias, we limited self-reporting of medication use to the past 6 months and used visual aids like medication pictures to assist recall. Where possible, prescriptions or medicine packaging were verified. Breastfeeding was defined broadly to include all practices incorporating breast milk, such as exclusive breastfeeding (EBF), complementary breastfeeding (CBF), and expressed breast milk feeding. Medicines were defined as all prescribed and non-prescribed medicines, including oral contraceptives and herbs. Participants were categorized into four groups based on their breastfeeding and medicine use history: (1) women who used medication while breastfeeding and were still breastfeeding at the time of the study, (2) women who used medication while breastfeeding but had stopped breastfeeding within the past three months, (3) women who did not use any medication during their breastfeeding period, and (4) women who discontinued breastfeeding due to medication use. Women who had stopped breastfeeding within the previous three months were included to capture recent medication use and breastfeeding practices to allow for a more comprehensive understanding of medication use during the breastfeeding period, including the immediate postpartum phase. The availability of safety information for medicines and the Relative Infant Dose (RID) was evaluated according to the LactMed database, Hales Lactation Risk Category, and the World Health Organization (WHO) Anatomic Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification system [ , ]. Also, RID values were used to estimate infant exposure to medications through breast milk. RID was calculated as: RID (%) = (Maternal dose (mg/kg/day)/Infant dose via milk (mg/kg/day) ​ × 100. Specifically, medications with a Relative Infant Dose (RID) of less than 10% were considered generally safe for breastfeeding; those with a RID between 10% and 25% were to be used with caution, depending on the drug class and the infant’s health status; and medications with a RID greater than 25% were considered potentially unsafe and generally not recommended during breastfeeding. Safety classification was further informed by data from Hale’s Medications and Mothers’ Milk, the LactMed database, and available pharmacokinetic studies. Based on these sources, medications were categorized as compatible, probably compatible, presumed compatible, possibly hazardous, and Hazardous. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participants’ characteristics. For categorical variables, frequencies and percentages were reported. The prevalence of medication use during breastfeeding was defined as the proportion of participants who had either used medication during their breastfeeding period or were actively using medication at the time of recruitment. A modified Poisson regression model was fitted to identify factors associated with medicine use among breastfeeding women. Factors were selected for the adjusted model if p < 0.2 at the univariate level, as well as based on clinical significance. A variable was considered statistically significant if the p-value was less than 0.05, and for prevalence ratios (PRs), statistical significance was confirmed when the 95% confidence interval did not include 1.0. In the regression model, the association of medication use with the following factors was examined: maternal age, infant age, education level, employment status, marital status, alcohol intake, smoking, mode of delivery for the last baby, presence of a current non-chronic medical condition, chronic condition (non-HIV), and HIV status. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize medication categories, lactation risk, relative infant dose (RID), and breastfeeding recommendations for participants taking medication while breastfeeding. Percentages of medication use were calculated by dividing the number of participants who reported using each specific medication by the total sample size (N = 294) and multiplying the result by 100. Among 132 participants who reported a current chronic condition (including HIV, hypertension, TB, and asthma), the majority were on condition-specific medications. Discussion This study revealed that more than 70% of the breastfeeding mothers attending six facilities in Kampala consumed medications, and more than 50% obtained drugs without prescriptions. Women with younger infants, higher education, or current acute conditions were more likely to use medications. The most commonly used antibiotics were metronidazole, used by 46.6% of women, which has a high RID dose of 11–24%, followed by amoxicillin and ampicillin/cloxacillin, taken by 38.1%, with low exposure to the infant through breastmilk, indicating safe compatibility. This study revealed that women with younger infants, higher education levels, or current acute conditions were more likely to use medications. The higher medication use among mothers of younger infants may be attributed to increased postpartum vulnerability and susceptibility to infections, as previously observed in maternal health studies [ , ]. This period often includes physiological and psychological adjustments, which can lead to increased healthcare-seeking behavior and medication intake to maintain the mother’s ability to care for the newborn. Women with younger infants may prioritize their health to maintain optimal care for their infants, leading to increased medication use. Similarly, higher education levels were associated with increased medication use, which may reflect better access to healthcare information and greater awareness of the need for treatment. Likewise, the association between higher education and medication use could reflect improved health literacy and greater access to healthcare services. Educated women may be more likely to recognize symptoms requiring treatment and seek medical advice [ ]. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as other unmeasured factors such as socioeconomic status, healthcare access, or health literacy may also influence this relationship, as noted by Goldman et al. [ ]. Hence, further studies are needed to explore these potential pathways. Our study found that 57.1% of breastfeeding mothers reported exclusive breastfeeding without pumping or expressing milk. Our study found that 57.1% of breastfeeding mothers reported exclusive breastfeeding without pumping or expressing milk. This moderate adherence to exclusive breastfeeding is consistent with prior research, particularly among women balancing caregiving and economic responsibilities. For instance, Nabunya et al. reported a 42.8% prevalence of exclusive breastfeeding among women working in the informal sector, highlighting how employment pressures can reduce time for optimal breastfeeding [ ]. The absence of milk expression in our study could indicate limited awareness, cultural practices, limited awareness or access to pumping methods, which can help manage breastfeeding challenges, such as maintaining milk supply or balancing work demands. Examining exclusive breastfeeding in this study is important because it helps identify potential barriers, including employment pressures and lack of milk expression options, which may influence both breastfeeding continuity and safe medication use among breastfeeding women [ , ]. Encouraging safe and accessible milk expression options could enhance breastfeeding continuity for mothers facing time constraints or work obligations. A total of 64.4% of participants obtained medications without prescriptions, indicating widespread self-medication practices. These medicines were accessed from both regulated sources, such as pharmacies and drug shops, and unregulated sources, including informal vendors. While self-medication is common in Uganda due to cost and access barriers, unregulated medication use, particularly from informal vendors, poses additional risks such as counterfeit or substandard drugs. Also, widespread self-medication practices may expose infants to potentially harmful drug levels through breast milk and increase the risk of incorrect dosing, adverse effects, or drug interactions [ , ]. Sources of obtaining drugs included: local pharmacies, drug shops, and informal vendors, where over-the-counter sales are common. Furthermore, a notable portion of women (78.9%) reported recent medication use within the past six months, as observed in Nigeria, where over 95% of women consumed medicines while breastfeeding [ ]. In this study. 8.2% had never used medications while breastfeeding; however, while some breastfeeding women were comfortable using medicines when needed, 12.9% stopped breastfeeding while on antiretroviral therapy because of high viral load, which would increase the chances of HIV exposure to the infant, as recommended by the healthcare providers. Analgesics were the most frequently used medications among breastfeeding women, with paracetamol accounting for 74.5% of use. Its well-established safety profile, low relative infant dose, and compatibility with breastfeeding make it a common choice for managing pain and fever during lactation. This is consistent with other studies showing that analgesics and antipyretics are the most commonly used medications among breastfeeding women [ – ], making it one of the safest analgesics for breastfeeding mothers. However, formulations containing caffeine require cautious use due to their higher exposure to breastfed infants (7–18%), which could increase infant exposure to caffeine, potentially leading to irritability or sleep disturbances in infants [ ]. The extensive use of antibiotics, including amoxicillin and ampicillin/cloxacillin, also reflects a pattern of safe medication practices among breastfeeding women. These antibiotics are generally regarded as compatible with breastfeeding, and their low exposure to infants (0.5-1%) supports their safety profile, posing minimal risk of adverse effects to the infant. This is in line with studies from similar populations that show amoxicillin and cloxacillin were the most used antibiotics due to their safety profiles and effectiveness in treating maternal infections while minimizing infant exposure risks [ , ]. This study reveals varying safety levels across drug categories for breastfeeding women. While most categories, such as antiretrovirals, antihistamines, corticosteroids, and supplements, are deemed “compatible for use” and generally safe. Caution is warranted when prescribing antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, cotrimoxazole, metronidazole, levofloxacin) and antihypertensive medications (atenolol, losartan) to breastfeeding women, as these drug classes may pose potential risks to the breastfed infant, including gastrointestinal disturbances, alterations in gut microbiota, and possible cardiovascular or renal effects. Although metronidazole has been associated with potential risks to breastfed infants, including gastrointestinal disturbances and possible mutagenic effects in high doses, it remains an essential component of treatment for postpartum infections. Given its critical role in managing maternal health conditions and the limited availability of safer, equally effective alternatives, its use during breastfeeding is often necessary, with careful consideration of dosing and timing to minimize infant exposure. The limited availability of controlled studies conducted in this population underscores the need for careful consideration. These medications should only be administered if the potential benefits to the mother outweigh the potential risks to the infant. Antifungal drugs, such as griseofulvin, were flagged as “probably Compatible,” with limited safety data. Healthcare providers have a responsibility to inquire about breastfeeding and provide appropriate guidance before prescribing medications. Women reported receiving information mainly on dosing and timing of the drug. Despite these guidelines, breastfeeding women may be unaware of such precautions, and they may not always receive adequate information from their healthcare providers regarding the safe use of medications during lactation. Our findings are consistent with prior studies highlighting limited provider communication on medicine safety during breastfeeding. For instance, a study by Osemene and Lamikanra et al. in Nigeria reported that most breastfeeding women received insufficient guidance about medication use from health professionals and instead relied on advice from pharmacy attendants or peers [ ]. In India, Bhuvaraghan et al. found that more than 60% of lactating women were unaware of whether the drugs they consumed were safe for breastfeeding, attributing this knowledge gap to a lack of proper counseling from health professionals [ ]. Communication gaps between healthcare providers and breastfeeding mothers can lead to inappropriate medicine use, especially in low-resource settings. Studies from South Africa and Kenya report that conflicting advice from different healthcare providers often confuses, with some women stopping breastfeeding unnecessarily [ ]. Despite global guidelines, including those from the World Health Organization recommending clear and consistent communication on medication safety during lactation, implementation at the facility level remains weak in many LMICs. Limited provider training, lack of accessible reference materials, and poor integration of breastfeeding counseling into maternal care pathways all contribute to the ongoing challenges faced by breastfeeding women. The findings of this study highlight important public health concerns regarding medicine use among breastfeeding women in urban health settings. The high prevalence of medication use, often without prescriptions, emphasizes the need for strengthened regulation of drug access and enhanced community education to reduce risks associated with self-medication. There is a critical need to implement national policies that improve the regulation of over-the-counter drug sales, especially in informal outlets such as drug shops and unlicensed vendors. Public health education campaigns tailored to breastfeeding women, particularly those with younger infants and lower educational attainment, should be developed to raise awareness about the risks of inappropriate medicine use and the importance of consulting healthcare providers. Health systems must prioritize training for healthcare workers on the safety profiles of medicines during lactation, integrating this knowledge into routine maternal and child health services. Additionally, accessible, up-to-date clinical reference tools and communication strategies should be made available to support informed prescribing and improve provider-patient interactions. Strengthening pharmacovigilance systems to monitor medicine use and its impact on breastfeeding mothers and infants is essential for evidence-based policymaking. These measures, if implemented, could reduce unregulated medicine use, promote safer breastfeeding practices in Uganda and similar low-resource settings. Strengths and limitations This is the first study in Uganda to explore medication use among breastfeeding women. It provides essential data on medication use behaviors specific to breastfeeding women in a low-resource setting. As the first study on this topic in this country, this research establishes baseline data that can support national health policies and targeted interventions to promote safe medication use during breastfeeding. It also highlights the need for accessible information on medication safety. The study captures a significant proportion of breastfeeding women, offering a robust sample size that enhances the reliability and generalizability of the findings. Lastly, the study highlights the implications of self-medication practices for infant safety and maternal health, contributing to the broader global discussion on maternal pharmacovigilance. Lactation risk categories used have several limitations, including reliance on limited or low-quality evidence, subjectivity in risk assignment, and failure to account for individual variations such as infant age, feeding patterns, and maternal health. The factors often oversimplify complex risks, focus predominantly on infant safety without balancing maternal treatment needs, and may not be updated frequently to reflect new evidence. The study was conducted in a healthcare setting, unlike in unregistered drug shops, where most of the illegal medicines could be sold. Additionally, the lack of global consensus among classification systems leads to inconsistent recommendations, and over-reliance on these simplified categorizations can hinder case-specific clinical decision-making. This study used theoretical RID estimates to assess infant drug exposure, though these do not account for individual variability in drug transfer, absorption, or metabolism. Without pharmacokinetic measurements from breast milk or infants, exposure and safety assessments remain uncertain, highlighting the need for future studies incorporating direct pharmacokinetic data. The reliance on self-reported data may have introduced recall bias, particularly for past medication use, and social desirability bias, where participants may underreport self-medication or non-prescribed drug use. These biases could affect the accuracy of reported medication practices and exposure estimates. Future studies should consider validating self-reports with pharmacy records or clinical data to enhance reliability. Moreover, the study was conducted at healthcare facilities, which might limit generalizability to all breastfeeding women in Uganda, especially those in rural or remote areas who may have different healthcare access and practices. Conclusion This study found a high prevalence of medication use among breastfeeding women, with many obtaining medicines without prescriptions. While most medicines used were considered compatible with breastfeeding, some, such as metronidazole and caffeine-containing drugs, posed higher exposure risks for infants. The findings emphasize the need for clear, accessible guidance on safe medicine use during lactation, improved healthcare provider communication, and stronger regulation of over-the-counter drug access. We recommend that the Ministry of Health and the National Drug Authority (NDA) strengthen policies regulating the sale and distribution of medications, particularly over-the-counter drugs, to reduce self-medication risks among breastfeeding women. The Ministry of Health should also integrate breastfeeding-specific pharmacological guidance into routine maternal and child health services, including healthcare provider training and community education programs. Furthermore, collaboration with the Ministry of Education could support public awareness campaigns to improve health literacy around medication safety during breastfeeding. Addressing these gaps is essential to ensure the safe use of medicines while supporting continued breastfeeding. Further research is needed to strengthen safety data for medicines commonly used in low-resource settings.

Introduction Breastfeeding is one of the most effective practices for promoting child health and survival. The World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) guidelines advise initiating breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, followed by exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months [ ] while continued breastfeeding with complementary foods is recommended for up to two years and beyond [ ]. In Uganda, exclusive breastfeeding rates for the first 6 months range from 40 to 67%, although they vary by region [ – ]. However, as breastfeeding mothers frequently encounter health problems that may necessitate medication, such as postpartum pain, infections, and chronic conditions, they must make informed decisions about safe medication use to avoid potential adverse effects on their infants. Various factors, including healthcare access, education, cultural beliefs, and individual health status, can affect mothers’ medication choices. Medicine use can substantially influence breastfeeding patterns and duration [ ], as certain drugs may interfere with milk production, composition, or flow. Specifically, drugs such as diphenhydramine, pseudoephedrine, haloperidol, and furosemide have been shown to impact milk synthesis and secretion, potentially leading to reduced breastfeeding efficacy or, in some cases, cessation of breastfeeding [ ]. Moreover, there exists a substantial gap in the literature concerning the safety of drugs used during lactation [ ]. While some medications are considered compatible with breastfeeding, limited evidence is available to assess the risks associated with many commonly used drugs. In Uganda, medications that typically require a prescription in many parts of the world, such as antibiotics, diazepam, amitriptyline, and codeine, can be purchased over the counter. This practice may pose potential risks, including improper use, lack of professional guidance, and increased likelihood of adverse effects or antimicrobial resistance [ ]. Similarly, breastfeeding women may resort to self-medication practices, obtaining medications without prescriptions or professional guidance, despite the increasing awareness of the benefits of breastfeeding. Breastfeeding in the context of Human Immunodeficiency Virus/Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (HIV/AIDS) presents additional difficulties. Uganda has made significant progress in the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. National guidelines recommend that women living with HIV and on antiretroviral therapy (ART) exclusively breastfeed for the first six months, followed by continued breastfeeding with complementary feeding for at least 12 months, provided the mother remains adherent to ART. According to the 2023 Uganda Population-Based HIV Impact Assessment (UPHIA), the national HIV prevalence among pregnant and breastfeeding women was estimated at 7.0% [ , ]. ART adherence is critical during breastfeeding to reduce vertical transmission, and concerns about medicine compatibility with breastfeeding may influence medication adherence behaviors among women living with HIV. The topic of safe medication use among breastfeeding women remains under-researched, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) like Uganda. Studies in other populations have shown that commonly used medications among breastfeeding women include analgesics, antibiotics, and antipyretics, regarded as generally safe due to their low levels of transfer to breast milk and low percentage of the dose prescribed to the mother that is received by the infant known as the Relative Infant Doses (RIDs) [ , ]. The RID is calculated as the dose received by the infant through breast milk (mg/kg/day) divided by the maternal dose (mg/kg/day) and expressed as a percentage. A commonly accepted threshold is that a RID of less than 10% is generally considered safe for breastfeeding. In this study, safety classification was based on established international references, including the WHO guidelines, LactMed database, and peer-reviewed pharmacokinetic literature. This approach enables evidence-based categorization of commonly used drugs as compatible, use with caution, or not recommended during breastfeeding. Studies have highlighted that self-medication practices are prevalent among breastfeeding mothers, especially in settings with limited access to healthcare, where women may obtain medications informally without prescriptions. In these settings, many medications requiring a prescription are available over the counter [ , ]. This study contributes to the existing body of evidence by offering specific understandings into medicine use during breastfeeding in Uganda, an area with limited research despite high breastfeeding rates and widespread access to over-the-counter medications. Unlike previous studies that have largely drawn from high-income countries. In particular, the study builds upon recent WHO and UNICEF guidance on breastfeeding by exploring how medication practices influence adherence to exclusive breastfeeding recommendations and duration. Likewise, by identifying commonly used drugs and evaluating their safety profiles, especially in a setting where prescription-only medicines are readily available over the counter, this study generates evidence critical for informing local health policy, clinical decision-making, and public health interventions tailored to breastfeeding mothers in Uganda and comparable LMIC settings. Given these considerations, the study aimed to investigate the prevalence of medicine use, evidence about safety, and factors that influence medicine use among breastfeeding women. Materials and methods Study design and setting This was a cross-sectional study conducted among breastfeeding women attending selected urban healthcare clinics in Kampala, Uganda. The study population included breastfeeding women aged 18 years and older, regardless of HIV status, to capture a comprehensive picture of medication use in this group. Data were collected from six healthcare clinics in Kampala, including the Infectious Diseases Institute (IDI) and Kampala City Council Authority (KCCA) affiliated clinics. These facilities provide a range of free maternal and child health services such as immunization, outpatient and inpatient care, and specialized treatment for people living with HIV. The IDI, a research institution linked to Makerere University’s College of Health Sciences, supports over 200,000 individuals living with HIV through its Health Systems Strengthening Programme. The KCCA clinics serve a diverse urban population of more than half a million people, offering comprehensive healthcare services including maternal and child health (MCH), infant immunizations, growth monitoring, family planning, and general health check-ups. Additionally, these clinics provide health education and counseling, which create opportunities to engage mothers on breastfeeding practices and medication use. Recruiting participants from these sites enabled access to a representative sample of breastfeeding women actively utilizing child health services in urban Kampala. Patient and public involvement The questionnaires were designed and piloted by the investigators and subsequently subjected to user testing by peer mothers affiliated with sexual and reproductive health clinics. This testing aimed to assess the questionnaires’ content, length, and usability, specifically among breastfeeding women. Peer mothers provided crucial feedback during this process, which informed multiple revisions of the questionnaires to enhance clarity and relevance. Beyond the piloting phase, peer mothers played vital roles in providing emotional support, educating breastfeeding women about medication safety, facilitating study participation, promoting adherence to study protocols, and fostering community engagement. Regular meetings with Community Advisory Board (CAB) members and peer mothers were held throughout the study to monitor progress and gather ongoing feedback, strengthening the collaboration between researchers and the community. The involvement of community members, peer mothers, and the CAB has been shown to effectively bridge gaps between researchers and the community, ensuring that study activities remain responsive to community needs [ , ]. These sessions provided a platform for feedback on study implementation. The questionnaires were also reviewed by the authors (LA, CW, RK), and multiple revisions were made to integrate user feedback. Eligibility and recruitment Breastfeeding women aged 18 years and above, irrespective of HIV status, with infants aged 12 months or younger, were included in the study. The women were recruited from MCH clinics located within six urban healthcare facilities across the selected study sites. This infant age range was selected because infants in this stage rely heavily on breast milk for nutrition, and maternal medication use could pose a higher risk of transfer through breast milk. Participants were recruited between September 2023 and January 2024 using systematic random sampling. Based on average clinic attendance, every 5th eligible woman was approached for participation. A total of 294 participants were recruited across six health facilities, with approximately 30 to 31 participants enrolled per site. Since all participating sites had comparable patient volumes, an equal allocation strategy was applied to ensure uniform representation from each facility. The first participant was randomly selected using a lottery method to ensure fairness and reduce selection bias. A total sample size of 294 participants was determined based on the assumption that 80% of breastfeeding women use medicines, a 95% confidence level, a 5% margin of error, and a design effect of 1.0, considering the use of systematic random sampling [ ]. The sample size was calculated using the formula for estimating a single population proportion: n = Z 2 ×p× (1-p)/d 2 . Where: n = required sample size, Z = Z-score corresponding to the desired confidence level (1.96 for 95%), p = estimated prevalence of medication use among breastfeeding women (assumed 80% or 0.8), d = margin of error (set at 0.05). An additional 5% was added to account for potential non-response or incomplete data. These parameters were chosen to ensure adequate precision in estimating the prevalence of medicine use and sufficient power to detect statistically significant associations in the analysis. Data collection procedures The survey questionnaire was developed based on insights from a comprehensive literature review and previously published surveys (1, 2). It was administered face-to-face to potential participants, and a series of structured questions was designed to be completed within 40 min. The questionnaire was professionally translated into Luganda, the most commonly spoken language in the selected study sites. Research assistants were trained to administer the questionnaire. The questionnaire gathered information on demographic characteristics (e.g., maternal age, education level, parity, and child’s age), types of medicines used, and breastfeeding practices. HIV status was self-reported by participants and, where possible, verified using clinic records. No additional HIV testing was conducted during the study, as all participants were recruited from healthcare facilities where HIV testing is routinely provided as part of maternal-child health services. To minimize recall bias, we limited self-reporting of medication use to the past 6 months and used visual aids like medication pictures to assist recall. Where possible, prescriptions or medicine packaging were verified. Breastfeeding was defined broadly to include all practices incorporating breast milk, such as exclusive breastfeeding (EBF), complementary breastfeeding (CBF), and expressed breast milk feeding. Medicines were defined as all prescribed and non-prescribed medicines, including oral contraceptives and herbs. Participants were categorized into four groups based on their breastfeeding and medicine use history: (1) women who used medication while breastfeeding and were still breastfeeding at the time of the study, (2) women who used medication while breastfeeding but had stopped breastfeeding within the past three months, (3) women who did not use any medication during their breastfeeding period, and (4) women who discontinued breastfeeding due to medication use. Women who had stopped breastfeeding within the previous three months were included to capture recent medication use and breastfeeding practices to allow for a more comprehensive understanding of medication use during the breastfeeding period, including the immediate postpartum phase. The availability of safety information for medicines and the Relative Infant Dose (RID) was evaluated according to the LactMed database, Hales Lactation Risk Category, and the World Health Organization (WHO) Anatomic Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification system [ , ]. Also, RID values were used to estimate infant exposure to medications through breast milk. RID was calculated as: RID (%) = (Maternal dose (mg/kg/day)/Infant dose via milk (mg/kg/day) ​ × 100. Specifically, medications with a Relative Infant Dose (RID) of less than 10% were considered generally safe for breastfeeding; those with a RID between 10% and 25% were to be used with caution, depending on the drug class and the infant’s health status; and medications with a RID greater than 25% were considered potentially unsafe and generally not recommended during breastfeeding. Safety classification was further informed by data from Hale’s Medications and Mothers’ Milk, the LactMed database, and available pharmacokinetic studies. Based on these sources, medications were categorized as compatible, probably compatible, presumed compatible, possibly hazardous, and Hazardous. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participants’ characteristics. For categorical variables, frequencies and percentages were reported. The prevalence of medication use during breastfeeding was defined as the proportion of participants who had either used medication during their breastfeeding period or were actively using medication at the time of recruitment. A modified Poisson regression model was fitted to identify factors associated with medicine use among breastfeeding women. Factors were selected for the adjusted model if p < 0.2 at the univariate level, as well as based on clinical significance. A variable was considered statistically significant if the p-value was less than 0.05, and for prevalence ratios (PRs), statistical significance was confirmed when the 95% confidence interval did not include 1.0. In the regression model, the association of medication use with the following factors was examined: maternal age, infant age, education level, employment status, marital status, alcohol intake, smoking, mode of delivery for the last baby, presence of a current non-chronic medical condition, chronic condition (non-HIV), and HIV status. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize medication categories, lactation risk, relative infant dose (RID), and breastfeeding recommendations for participants taking medication while breastfeeding. Percentages of medication use were calculated by dividing the number of participants who reported using each specific medication by the total sample size (N = 294) and multiplying the result by 100. Discussion This study revealed that more than 70% of the breastfeeding mothers attending six facilities in Kampala consumed medications, and more than 50% obtained drugs without prescriptions. Women with younger infants, higher education, or current acute conditions were more likely to use medications. The most commonly used antibiotics were metronidazole, used by 46.6% of women, which has a high RID dose of 11–24%, followed by amoxicillin and ampicillin/cloxacillin, taken by 38.1%, with low exposure to the infant through breastmilk, indicating safe compatibility. This study revealed that women with younger infants, higher education levels, or current acute conditions were more likely to use medications. The higher medication use among mothers of younger infants may be attributed to increased postpartum vulnerability and susceptibility to infections, as previously observed in maternal health studies [ , ]. This period often includes physiological and psychological adjustments, which can lead to increased healthcare-seeking behavior and medication intake to maintain the mother’s ability to care for the newborn. Women with younger infants may prioritize their health to maintain optimal care for their infants, leading to increased medication use. Similarly, higher education levels were associated with increased medication use, which may reflect better access to healthcare information and greater awareness of the need for treatment. Likewise, the association between higher education and medication use could reflect improved health literacy and greater access to healthcare services. Educated women may be more likely to recognize symptoms requiring treatment and seek medical advice [ ]. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as other unmeasured factors such as socioeconomic status, healthcare access, or health literacy may also influence this relationship, as noted by Goldman et al. [ ]. Hence, further studies are needed to explore these potential pathways. Our study found that 57.1% of breastfeeding mothers reported exclusive breastfeeding without pumping or expressing milk. Our study found that 57.1% of breastfeeding mothers reported exclusive breastfeeding without pumping or expressing milk. This moderate adherence to exclusive breastfeeding is consistent with prior research, particularly among women balancing caregiving and economic responsibilities. For instance, Nabunya et al. reported a 42.8% prevalence of exclusive breastfeeding among women working in the informal sector, highlighting how employment pressures can reduce time for optimal breastfeeding [ ]. The absence of milk expression in our study could indicate limited awareness, cultural practices, limited awareness or access to pumping methods, which can help manage breastfeeding challenges, such as maintaining milk supply or balancing work demands. Examining exclusive breastfeeding in this study is important because it helps identify potential barriers, including employment pressures and lack of milk expression options, which may influence both breastfeeding continuity and safe medication use among breastfeeding women [ , ]. Encouraging safe and accessible milk expression options could enhance breastfeeding continuity for mothers facing time constraints or work obligations. A total of 64.4% of participants obtained medications without prescriptions, indicating widespread self-medication practices. These medicines were accessed from both regulated sources, such as pharmacies and drug shops, and unregulated sources, including informal vendors. While self-medication is common in Uganda due to cost and access barriers, unregulated medication use, particularly from informal vendors, poses additional risks such as counterfeit or substandard drugs. Also, widespread self-medication practices may expose infants to potentially harmful drug levels through breast milk and increase the risk of incorrect dosing, adverse effects, or drug interactions [ , ]. Sources of obtaining drugs included: local pharmacies, drug shops, and informal vendors, where over-the-counter sales are common. Furthermore, a notable portion of women (78.9%) reported recent medication use within the past six months, as observed in Nigeria, where over 95% of women consumed medicines while breastfeeding [ ]. In this study. 8.2% had never used medications while breastfeeding; however, while some breastfeeding women were comfortable using medicines when needed, 12.9% stopped breastfeeding while on antiretroviral therapy because of high viral load, which would increase the chances of HIV exposure to the infant, as recommended by the healthcare providers. Analgesics were the most frequently used medications among breastfeeding women, with paracetamol accounting for 74.5% of use. Its well-established safety profile, low relative infant dose, and compatibility with breastfeeding make it a common choice for managing pain and fever during lactation. This is consistent with other studies showing that analgesics and antipyretics are the most commonly used medications among breastfeeding women [ – ], making it one of the safest analgesics for breastfeeding mothers. However, formulations containing caffeine require cautious use due to their higher exposure to breastfed infants (7–18%), which could increase infant exposure to caffeine, potentially leading to irritability or sleep disturbances in infants [ ]. The extensive use of antibiotics, including amoxicillin and ampicillin/cloxacillin, also reflects a pattern of safe medication practices among breastfeeding women. These antibiotics are generally regarded as compatible with breastfeeding, and their low exposure to infants (0.5-1%) supports their safety profile, posing minimal risk of adverse effects to the infant. This is in line with studies from similar populations that show amoxicillin and cloxacillin were the most used antibiotics due to their safety profiles and effectiveness in treating maternal infections while minimizing infant exposure risks [ , ]. This study reveals varying safety levels across drug categories for breastfeeding women. While most categories, such as antiretrovirals, antihistamines, corticosteroids, and supplements, are deemed “compatible for use” and generally safe. Caution is warranted when prescribing antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, cotrimoxazole, metronidazole, levofloxacin) and antihypertensive medications (atenolol, losartan) to breastfeeding women, as these drug classes may pose potential risks to the breastfed infant, including gastrointestinal disturbances, alterations in gut microbiota, and possible cardiovascular or renal effects. Although metronidazole has been associated with potential risks to breastfed infants, including gastrointestinal disturbances and possible mutagenic effects in high doses, it remains an essential component of treatment for postpartum infections. Given its critical role in managing maternal health conditions and the limited availability of safer, equally effective alternatives, its use during breastfeeding is often necessary, with careful consideration of dosing and timing to minimize infant exposure. The limited availability of controlled studies conducted in this population underscores the need for careful consideration. These medications should only be administered if the potential benefits to the mother outweigh the potential risks to the infant. Antifungal drugs, such as griseofulvin, were flagged as “probably Compatible,” with limited safety data. Likewise, Yevgenia et al. evaluated the strength of the data for the most commonly administered medications in lactating women and found that 51% of medicines had no associated data, 664 (47%) had minimal-moderate data, and 30 (2%) had strong data using the LactMed database and WHO classification [ ]. Antifungal drugs, such as griseofulvin, were flagged as “probably Compatible,” with limited safety data. Likewise, Yevgenia et al. evaluated the strength of the data for the most commonly administered medications in lactating women and found that 51% of medicines had no associated data, 664 (47%) had minimal-moderate data, and 30 (2%) had strong data using the LactMed database and WHO classification [ ]. For medicines that are flagged for cautious use, it is generally recommended to adjust or avoid breastfeeding for 2–4 h following administration. However, for certain medications such as cotrimoxazole, it is advised to avoid breastfeeding in infants with G6PD deficiency, regardless of the standard recommendations. However, routine screening for G6PD deficiency remains uncommon in many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), making it challenging to implement such targeted precautions in clinical practice. Nevertheless, women reported a lack of guidance from healthcare providers regarding breastfeeding adjustments while on certain medications. Furthermore, some women did not disclose their breastfeeding status to healthcare providers, highlighting a mutual gap in communication. Healthcare providers have a responsibility to inquire about breastfeeding and provide appropriate guidance before prescribing medications. Women reported receiving information mainly on dosing and timing of the drug. Despite these guidelines, breastfeeding women may be unaware of such precautions, and they may not always receive adequate information from their healthcare providers regarding the safe use of medications during lactation. Our findings are consistent with prior studies highlighting limited provider communication on medicine safety during breastfeeding. For instance, a study by Osemene and Lamikanra et al. in Nigeria reported that most breastfeeding women received insufficient guidance about medication use from health professionals and instead relied on advice from pharmacy attendants or peers [ ]. In India, Bhuvaraghan et al. found that more than 60% of lactating women were unaware of whether the drugs they consumed were safe for breastfeeding, attributing this knowledge gap to a lack of proper counseling from health professionals [ ]. Communication gaps between healthcare providers and breastfeeding mothers can lead to inappropriate medicine use, especially in low-resource settings. Studies from South Africa and Kenya report that conflicting advice from different healthcare providers often confuses, with some women stopping breastfeeding unnecessarily [ ]. Despite global guidelines, including those from the World Health Organization recommending clear and consistent communication on medication safety during lactation, implementation at the facility level remains weak in many LMICs. Limited provider training, lack of accessible reference materials, and poor integration of breastfeeding counseling into maternal care pathways all contribute to the ongoing challenges faced by breastfeeding women. The findings of this study highlight important public health concerns regarding medicine use among breastfeeding women in urban health settings. The high prevalence of medication use, often without prescriptions, emphasizes the need for strengthened regulation of drug access and enhanced community education to reduce risks associated with self-medication. There is a critical need to implement national policies that improve the regulation of over-the-counter drug sales, especially in informal outlets such as drug shops and unlicensed vendors. Public health education campaigns tailored to breastfeeding women, particularly those with younger infants and lower educational attainment, should be developed to raise awareness about the risks of inappropriate medicine use and the importance of consulting healthcare providers. Health systems must prioritize training for healthcare workers on the safety profiles of medicines during lactation, integrating this knowledge into routine maternal and child health services. Additionally, accessible, up-to-date clinical reference tools and communication strategies should be made available to support informed prescribing and improve provider-patient interactions. Strengthening pharmacovigilance systems to monitor medicine use and its impact on breastfeeding mothers and infants is essential for evidence-based policymaking. These measures, if implemented, could reduce unregulated medicine use, promote safer breastfeeding practices in Uganda and similar low-resource settings. Strengths and limitations This is the first study in Uganda to explore medication use among breastfeeding women. It provides essential data on medication use behaviors specific to breastfeeding women in a low-resource setting. As the first study on this topic in this country, this research establishes baseline data that can support national health policies and targeted interventions to promote safe medication use during breastfeeding. It also highlights the need for accessible information on medication safety. The study captures a significant proportion of breastfeeding women, offering a robust sample size that enhances the reliability and generalizability of the findings. Lastly, the study highlights the implications of self-medication practices for infant safety and maternal health, contributing to the broader global discussion on maternal pharmacovigilance. Lactation risk categories used have several limitations, including reliance on limited or low-quality evidence, subjectivity in risk assignment, and failure to account for individual variations such as infant age, feeding patterns, and maternal health. Lactation risk categories used have several limitations, including reliance on limited or low-quality evidence, subjectivity in risk assignment, and failure to account for individual variations such as infant age, feeding patterns, and maternal health. The factors often oversimplify complex risks, focus predominantly on infant safety without balancing maternal treatment needs, and may not be updated frequently to reflect new evidence. The study was conducted in a healthcare setting, unlike in unregistered drug shops, where most of the illegal medicines could be sold. Additionally, the lack of global consensus among classification systems leads to inconsistent recommendations, and over-reliance on these simplified categorizations can hinder case-specific clinical decision-making. This study used theoretical RID estimates to assess infant drug exposure, though these do not account for individual variability in drug transfer, absorption, or metabolism. Without pharmacokinetic measurements from breast milk or infants, exposure and safety assessments remain uncertain, highlighting the need for future studies incorporating direct pharmacokinetic data. The reliance on self-reported data may have introduced recall bias, particularly for past medication use, and social desirability bias, where participants may underreport self-medication or non-prescribed drug use. These biases could affect the accuracy of reported medication practices and exposure estimates. Future studies should consider validating self-reports with pharmacy records or clinical data to enhance reliability. Moreover, the study was conducted at healthcare facilities, which might limit generalizability to all breastfeeding women in Uganda, especially those in rural or remote areas who may have different healthcare access and practices. Conclusion This study found a high prevalence of medication use among breastfeeding women, with many obtaining medicines without prescriptions. While most medicines used were considered compatible with breastfeeding, some, such as metronidazole and caffeine-containing drugs, posed higher exposure risks for infants. The findings emphasize the need for clear, accessible guidance on safe medicine use during lactation, improved healthcare provider communication, and stronger regulation of over-the-counter drug access. We recommend that the Ministry of Health and the National Drug Authority (NDA) strengthen policies regulating the sale and distribution of medications, particularly over-the-counter drugs, to reduce self-medication risks among breastfeeding women. The Ministry of Health should also integrate breastfeeding-specific pharmacological guidance into routine maternal and child health services, including healthcare provider training and community education programs. Furthermore, collaboration with the Ministry of Education could support public awareness campaigns to improve health literacy around medication safety during breastfeeding. Addressing these gaps is essential to ensure the safe use of medicines while supporting continued breastfeeding. Further research is needed to strengthen safety data for medicines commonly used in low-resource settings.

Introduction Breastfeeding is one of the most effective practices for promoting child health and survival. The World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) guidelines advise initiating breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, followed by exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months [ ] while continued breastfeeding with complementary foods is recommended for up to two years and beyond [ ]. In Uganda, exclusive breastfeeding rates for the first 6 months range from 40 to 67%, although they vary by region [ – ]. However, as breastfeeding mothers frequently encounter health problems that may necessitate medication, such as postpartum pain, infections, and chronic conditions, they must make informed decisions about safe medication use to avoid potential adverse effects on their infants. Various factors, including healthcare access, education, cultural beliefs, and individual health status, can affect mothers’ medication choices. Medicine use can substantially influence breastfeeding patterns and duration [ ], as certain drugs may interfere with milk production, composition, or flow. Specifically, drugs such as diphenhydramine, pseudoephedrine, haloperidol, and furosemide have been shown to impact milk synthesis and secretion, potentially leading to reduced breastfeeding efficacy or, in some cases, cessation of breastfeeding [ ]. Moreover, there exists a substantial gap in the literature concerning the safety of drugs used during lactation [ ]. While some medications are considered compatible with breastfeeding, limited evidence is available to assess the risks associated with many commonly used drugs. In Uganda, medications that typically require a prescription in many parts of the world, such as antibiotics, diazepam, amitriptyline, and codeine, can be purchased over the counter. This practice may pose potential risks, including improper use, lack of professional guidance, and increased likelihood of adverse effects or antimicrobial resistance [ ]. Similarly, breastfeeding women may resort to self-medication practices, obtaining medications without prescriptions or professional guidance, despite the increasing awareness of the benefits of breastfeeding. Breastfeeding in the context of Human Immunodeficiency Virus/Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (HIV/AIDS) presents additional difficulties. Uganda has made significant progress in the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. National guidelines recommend that women living with HIV and on antiretroviral therapy (ART) exclusively breastfeed for the first six months, followed by continued breastfeeding with complementary feeding for at least 12 months, provided the mother remains adherent to ART. According to the 2023 Uganda Population-Based HIV Impact Assessment (UPHIA), the national HIV prevalence among pregnant and breastfeeding women was estimated at 7.0% [ , ]. ART adherence is critical during breastfeeding to reduce vertical transmission, and concerns about medicine compatibility with breastfeeding may influence medication adherence behaviors among women living with HIV. The topic of safe medication use among breastfeeding women remains under-researched, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) like Uganda. Studies in other populations have shown that commonly used medications among breastfeeding women include analgesics, antibiotics, and antipyretics, regarded as generally safe due to their low levels of transfer to breast milk and low percentage of the dose prescribed to the mother that is received by the infant known as the Relative Infant Doses (RIDs) [ , ]. The RID is calculated as the dose received by the infant through breast milk (mg/kg/day) divided by the maternal dose (mg/kg/day) and expressed as a percentage. A commonly accepted threshold is that a RID of less than 10% is generally considered safe for breastfeeding. In this study, safety classification was based on established international references, including the WHO guidelines, LactMed database, and peer-reviewed pharmacokinetic literature. This approach enables evidence-based categorization of commonly used drugs as compatible, use with caution, or not recommended during breastfeeding. Studies have highlighted that self-medication practices are prevalent among breastfeeding mothers, especially in settings with limited access to healthcare, where women may obtain medications informally without prescriptions. In these settings, many medications requiring a prescription are available over the counter [ , ]. This study contributes to the existing body of evidence by offering specific understandings into medicine use during breastfeeding in Uganda, an area with limited research despite high breastfeeding rates and widespread access to over-the-counter medications. Unlike previous studies that have largely drawn from high-income countries. In particular, the study builds upon recent WHO and UNICEF guidance on breastfeeding by exploring how medication practices influence adherence to exclusive breastfeeding recommendations and duration. Likewise, by identifying commonly used drugs and evaluating their safety profiles, especially in a setting where prescription-only medicines are readily available over the counter, this study generates evidence critical for informing local health policy, clinical decision-making, and public health interventions tailored to breastfeeding mothers in Uganda and comparable LMIC settings. Given these considerations, the study aimed to investigate the prevalence of medicine use, evidence about safety, and factors that influence medicine use among breastfeeding women. Materials and methods Study design and setting This was a cross-sectional study conducted among breastfeeding women attending selected urban healthcare clinics in Kampala, Uganda. The study population included breastfeeding women aged 18 years and older, regardless of HIV status, to capture a comprehensive picture of medication use in this group. Data were collected from six healthcare clinics in Kampala, including the Infectious Diseases Institute (IDI) and Kampala City Council Authority (KCCA) affiliated clinics. These facilities provide a range of free maternal and child health services such as immunization, outpatient and inpatient care, and specialized treatment for people living with HIV. The IDI, a research institution linked to Makerere University’s College of Health Sciences, supports over 200,000 individuals living with HIV through its Health Systems Strengthening Programme. The KCCA clinics serve a diverse urban population of more than half a million people, offering comprehensive healthcare services including maternal and child health (MCH), infant immunizations, growth monitoring, family planning, and general health check-ups. Additionally, these clinics provide health education and counseling, which create opportunities to engage mothers on breastfeeding practices and medication use. Recruiting participants from these sites enabled access to a representative sample of breastfeeding women actively utilizing child health services in urban Kampala. Patient and public involvement The questionnaires were designed and piloted by the investigators and subsequently subjected to user testing by peer mothers affiliated with sexual and reproductive health clinics. This testing aimed to assess the questionnaires’ content, length, and usability, specifically among breastfeeding women. Peer mothers provided crucial feedback during this process, which informed multiple revisions of the questionnaires to enhance clarity and relevance. Beyond the piloting phase, peer mothers played vital roles in providing emotional support, educating breastfeeding women about medication safety, facilitating study participation, promoting adherence to study protocols, and fostering community engagement. Regular meetings with Community Advisory Board (CAB) members and peer mothers were held throughout the study to monitor progress and gather ongoing feedback, strengthening the collaboration between researchers and the community. The involvement of community members, peer mothers, and the CAB has been shown to effectively bridge gaps between researchers and the community, ensuring that study activities remain responsive to community needs [ , ]. These sessions provided a platform for feedback on study implementation. The questionnaires were also reviewed by the authors (LA, CW, RK), and multiple revisions were made to integrate user feedback. Eligibility and recruitment Breastfeeding women aged 18 years and above, irrespective of HIV status, with infants aged 12 months or younger, were included in the study. The women were recruited from MCH clinics located within six urban healthcare facilities across the selected study sites. This infant age range was selected because infants in this stage rely heavily on breast milk for nutrition, and maternal medication use could pose a higher risk of transfer through breast milk. Participants were recruited between September 2023 and January 2024 using systematic random sampling. Based on average clinic attendance, every 5th eligible woman was approached for participation. A total of 294 participants were recruited across six health facilities, with approximately 30 to 31 participants enrolled per site. Since all participating sites had comparable patient volumes, an equal allocation strategy was applied to ensure uniform representation from each facility. The first participant was randomly selected using a lottery method to ensure fairness and reduce selection bias. A total sample size of 294 participants was determined based on the assumption that 80% of breastfeeding women use medicines, a 95% confidence level, a 5% margin of error, and a design effect of 1.0, considering the use of systematic random sampling [ ]. The sample size was calculated using the formula for estimating a single population proportion: n = Z 2 ×p× (1-p)/d 2 . Where: n = required sample size, Z = Z-score corresponding to the desired confidence level (1.96 for 95%), p = estimated prevalence of medication use among breastfeeding women (assumed 80% or 0.8), d = margin of error (set at 0.05). An additional 5% was added to account for potential non-response or incomplete data. These parameters were chosen to ensure adequate precision in estimating the prevalence of medicine use and sufficient power to detect statistically significant associations in the analysis. Data collection procedures The survey questionnaire was developed based on insights from a comprehensive literature review and previously published surveys (1, 2). It was administered face-to-face to potential participants, and a series of structured questions was designed to be completed within 40 min. The questionnaire was professionally translated into Luganda, the most commonly spoken language in the selected study sites. Research assistants were trained to administer the questionnaire. The questionnaire gathered information on demographic characteristics (e.g., maternal age, education level, parity, and child’s age), types of medicines used, and breastfeeding practices. HIV status was self-reported by participants and, where possible, verified using clinic records. No additional HIV testing was conducted during the study, as all participants were recruited from healthcare facilities where HIV testing is routinely provided as part of maternal-child health services. To minimize recall bias, we limited self-reporting of medication use to the past 6 months and used visual aids like medication pictures to assist recall. Where possible, prescriptions or medicine packaging were verified. Breastfeeding was defined broadly to include all practices incorporating breast milk, such as exclusive breastfeeding (EBF), complementary breastfeeding (CBF), and expressed breast milk feeding. Medicines were defined as all prescribed and non-prescribed medicines, including oral contraceptives and herbs. Participants were categorized into four groups based on their breastfeeding and medicine use history: (1) women who used medication while breastfeeding and were still breastfeeding at the time of the study, (2) women who used medication while breastfeeding but had stopped breastfeeding within the past three months, (3) women who did not use any medication during their breastfeeding period, and (4) women who discontinued breastfeeding due to medication use. Women who had stopped breastfeeding within the previous three months were included to capture recent medication use and breastfeeding practices to allow for a more comprehensive understanding of medication use during the breastfeeding period, including the immediate postpartum phase. The availability of safety information for medicines and the Relative Infant Dose (RID) was evaluated according to the LactMed database, Hales Lactation Risk Category, and the World Health Organization (WHO) Anatomic Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification system [ , ]. Also, RID values were used to estimate infant exposure to medications through breast milk. RID was calculated as: RID (%) = (Maternal dose (mg/kg/day)/Infant dose via milk (mg/kg/day) ​ × 100. Specifically, medications with a Relative Infant Dose (RID) of less than 10% were considered generally safe for breastfeeding; those with a RID between 10% and 25% were to be used with caution, depending on the drug class and the infant’s health status; and medications with a RID greater than 25% were considered potentially unsafe and generally not recommended during breastfeeding. Safety classification was further informed by data from Hale’s Medications and Mothers’ Milk, the LactMed database, and available pharmacokinetic studies. Based on these sources, medications were categorized as compatible, probably compatible, presumed compatible, possibly hazardous, and Hazardous. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participants’ characteristics. For categorical variables, frequencies and percentages were reported. The prevalence of medication use during breastfeeding was defined as the proportion of participants who had either used medication during their breastfeeding period or were actively using medication at the time of recruitment. A modified Poisson regression model was fitted to identify factors associated with medicine use among breastfeeding women. Factors were selected for the adjusted model if p < 0.2 at the univariate level, as well as based on clinical significance. A variable was considered statistically significant if the p-value was less than 0.05, and for prevalence ratios (PRs), statistical significance was confirmed when the 95% confidence interval did not include 1.0. In the regression model, the association of medication use with the following factors was examined: maternal age, infant age, education level, employment status, marital status, alcohol intake, smoking, mode of delivery for the last baby, presence of a current non-chronic medical condition, chronic condition (non-HIV), and HIV status. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize medication categories, lactation risk, relative infant dose (RID), and breastfeeding recommendations for participants taking medication while breastfeeding. Percentages of medication use were calculated by dividing the number of participants who reported using each specific medication by the total sample size (N = 294) and multiplying the result by 100.
