The study aim was to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the prevalence of breastfeeding initiation and continuation until 6 months post partum while on medication. Methods Patient and public involvement Patients and the public were not involved in this systematic review as it was based on an analysis of previously published studies. The findings aim to inform patient-centred care and future research involving patients and the public. Search strategy The study protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42024541470) on 13 May 2024. The systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Protocol. The systematic review included all completed and published studies involving pregnant and breastfeeding women who reported medicine use or drug use, including but not limited to antidepressants, antihypertensives, antipsychotics, antiretroviral drugs, antihypertensives and in some cases, studies that assessed overall medicine use without specifying individual drug classes. We studied any measure of exclusive breastfeeding, breastfeeding initiation or breastfeeding continuation. The search strategy was conducted on PubMed, Web of Science, Academic Search Premier (on the EBSCO Platform) and Google Scholar. A search was performed using medical subject headings and text words in PubMed and then adapted for Web of Science. We used “breastfeeding” along with its alternative words; “Nursing women” OR “nursing mothers” OR “breastfeeding women” OR “pregnant” OR “pregnant women”[Title/Abstract] OR “lactating mother” OR infant* OR neonate* OR “newborn babies” and other culturally specific terms as shown in the . The search included studies published until November 2024. The full search strategy for all databases is provided in . Eligibility criteria The systematic review included a broad range of study designs to ensure methodological inclusiveness and capture diverse sources of evidence. Eligible studies encompassed randomised clinical trials (RCTs), retrospective and prospective observational studies and cross-sectional quantitative studies. There were no geographical limitations imposed, allowing for global representation of the evidence base. Included studies specifically evaluated the influence of medication use on breastfeeding initiation and continuation up to 6 months post partum. Breastfeeding initiation refers to whether the mother began breastfeeding after birth, and exclusive initiation refers to whether breastfeeding was exclusive at the start, without supplementation. Breastfeeding continuation describes whether the mother was still breastfeeding at specific time points (eg, 3 or 6 months post partum), while duration captures the total length of breastfeeding, typically reported in weeks or months. The target population comprised postpartum women who were breastfeeding or had breastfed during the postpartum period. The review considered studies assessing the impact of medications, including antidepressants, antihypertensives, antiepileptic drugs, antipsychotics and anti-tuberculosis medications administered from pregnancy through the postpartum period. Selection criteria prioritised studies that demonstrated inclusiveness, practical applicability and methodological rigour. To ensure an inclusive and feasible systematic review, publications from 1997 to 2024 were considered for inclusion. This time frame was selected to maximise the breadth of relevant evidence. Abstracts presented at scientific meetings were not included due to a lack of detailed information. Reference lists from other reviews were examined to identify further eligible studies. To determine the suitability, the authors then retrieved the study abstracts and, if necessary, the full text of the articles. The web-based Rayyan software was used for this purpose. Accordingly, all publications available in all languages within the selected databases were reviewed. Studies were excluded if they focused exclusively on medicine use during pregnancy without assessing its implications for breastfeeding. Additionally, studies were omitted if they lacked direct relevance to the research questions and objectives of the systematic review. Specifically, the exclusion criteria encompassed studies reporting on medicine use solely in infants or pregnant women, those addressing medication use without linking it to breastfeeding outcomes, and animal studies, which were deemed insufficiently generalisable to human lactation contexts. Furthermore, non-primary research articles, including case reports, case series, commentaries, reviews, viewpoints and opinion pieces, were excluded to maintain the analytical rigour and relevance of the evidence base. Study selection and data extraction The study selection process was systematically executed using the Rayyan platform, employing a rigorous two-phase screening strategy. In the initial phase, titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (RN and IK) to determine preliminary eligibility based on the inclusion criteria. In the subsequent phase, full-text articles of studies identified as potentially eligible were retrieved by two reviewers and assessed in greater depth to confirm their suitability for inclusion. Following the removal of duplicate records, two independent reviewers (RN and IK) conducted the title and abstract screening to assess preliminary eligibility based on the inclusion criteria. To optimise efficiency and minimise bias, the references were randomly divided so that each reviewer independently screened half of the total citations. For citations where eligibility was uncertain, both reviewers jointly assessed the study to reach consensus. A study was included only if both reviewers independently or jointly deemed it eligible, and excluded if both agreed it did not meet the eligibility criteria. In cases of discordance between the primary reviewers regarding a study’s inclusion, a third reviewer (NK, a MILK study team member) was consulted to adjudicate and facilitate resolution through consensus. For studies with abstracts that were ambiguous or lacking sufficient detail, the full texts were retrieved to allow a more comprehensive assessment. This ensured that potentially relevant studies were not prematurely excluded. The overall selection process is illustrated in , which depicts the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) flow diagram, outlining the number of records identified, screened, deemed eligible and ultimately included in the final synthesis. Data extraction from the eligible studies was independently conducted by two reviewers (RN and IK) using a standardised data extraction form. Each reviewer extracted data in duplicate, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer to ensure accuracy and consistency. The following key information was systematically extracted from each study into an Excel spreadsheet: (1) study characteristics, including author(s), year of publication, country of origin and study design; (2) participant characteristics, such as sample size and population details; (3) outcomes measured; (4) results, including effect sizes (eg, prevalence rates), CIs and p values. Following data extraction, the final dataset was independently reviewed by RN and IK to ensure its accuracy and completeness before proceeding with statistical analysis. Study quality assessment Each of the studies was individually assessed for conformity with the best practices for reporting systematic reviews as recommended by the PRISMA guidelines. The 27 items/criteria of the PRISMA guidelines were relevant to 28 studies. The risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist. A decision was made to include, exclude or seek further information for each study. To ensure sufficient sensitivity in differentiating study quality, studies were classified as high quality: ≥85% ‘Yes’ responses. Moderate quality: 60%–84% ‘Yes’ responses. Low quality: <60% ‘Yes’ responses. These categorical thresholds are consistent with established approaches in systematic review quality scoring, where overall percentage scores are used to distinguish low, moderate and high quality in quality appraisal frameworks as seen in . Subgroup analyses were considered particularly useful for investigating heterogeneity, as pooled estimates derived from subgroups with low heterogeneity are more interpretable than overall estimates influenced by high heterogeneity. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Evidence was systematically appraised across five domains: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. In this review, the certainty of evidence was downgraded from ‘high’ to ‘low’ or ‘very low’ due to serious inconsistency, as evidenced by high statistical heterogeneity ( I ² >90%), and documented risk of publication bias regarding breastfeeding initiation. To investigate potential sources of heterogeneity, meta-regression analyses were conducted using the metareg package in Stata. Prespecified covariates included continent, country income status, HIV status of the population and drug class of medications taken during post partum. These variables were selected based on biological plausibility and prior literature. Publication bias and small-study effects were assessed using funnel plots, alongside formal statistical tests including Egger’s test and Begg’s rank correlation test, implemented via the metafunnel and metabias commands in Stata. Subgroup analyses were performed on the same covariates described above to explore the robustness of pooled estimates. All statistical tests were two-sided, and significance was defined as p<0.05 unless otherwise specified. The meta-analysis followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and adhered to recommendations from the Meta-analysis Of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) statement. Results Study selection A total of 286 records were identified through systematic database searches. After removing 47 duplicates, 239 unique records remained for screening. Following title and abstract screening, 126 records were excluded for not meeting the inclusion criteria. Of the 113 records sought for full-text retrieval, 65 reports were not included as they were not relevant to the study objectives; these included review articles, studies not conducted in humans and study protocols. The remaining 48 full-text articles were assessed in detail, resulting in the exclusion of 19 articles, 8 for not meeting eligibility criteria (eg, population or study design mismatch) and 11 for not reporting relevant breastfeeding outcomes. Finally, 29 studies were deemed eligible and included in the final systematic review; however, 1 study was excluded from the meta-analysis due to insufficient or incompatible data, resulting in 28 studies being included in the quantitative synthesis as detailed in . Study characteristics Of the 29 studies included in the review, 2 were randomised controlled trials, 14 were cohort studies and 13 were cross-sectional studies. Geographically, the studies were distributed as follows: 8 were conducted in Africa, 4 in Europe, 12 in the USA, 4 in Asia and 1 in Australia. By drug class, eight studies recruited women on antiretroviral therapy (ART), five studies were on antidepressants, one was on antihypertensives, four were on antiepileptics, two were on opioids, one was on systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and eight did not specify the type of medication, as illustrated in . Breastfeeding initiation The pooled prevalence of breastfeeding initiation among postpartum women on medication was 75.2% (95% CI 69.8% to 80.7%), derived from 28 studies involving 13 384 participants. This estimate was derived from a combination of standalone cross-sectional studies and baseline or follow-up cross-sectional data extracted from retrospective and prospective cohort studies and RCTs. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies ( I ²=99.2%, p<0.001) as indicated in . The lowest initiation rate was reported in a study involving women with SLE (36.7%), while the highest rate was observed in a study from an upper-middle-income country (96.1%). In subgroup analyses, breastfeeding initiation varied geographically, with the highest prevalence reported in Africa (84.3%; 95% CI 0.78% to 0.90%; k =08; I 2 =98.1%) and the lowest in Asia (66.2%; 95% CI 0.47% to 0.85%; k =04; I 2 =98.1%). Income level and drug class were identified as significant moderators. Women in high-income settings were significantly less likely to initiate breastfeeding compared with those in low-income settings (coefficient: −0.57, p<0.001), whereas women using antidepressants were more likely to initiate breastfeeding (coefficient: +0.50, p=0.008). Breastfeeding continuation up to 6 months The pooled prevalence of breastfeeding continuation up to 6 months post partum was 53.2% (95% CI 43.2% to 63.2%), based on 22 studies including 10 970 participants. The lowest continuation rate was reported among women who used opioids (23.6%), while the highest was among women on unspecified medications (74.0%). Heterogeneity was again substantial ( I ²=99.2%, p<0.001), indicating high variability across studies as illustrated in . In subgroup analyses, by continent, Africa had the highest breastfeeding continuation rate (66.6%). Asia (50.7%), Europe (47.3%) and America (43.8%) followed. By income level, lower-middle-income countries showed the highest continuation (79.8%), followed by low-income (62.2%). High-income countries had the lowest continuation rate (41.8%). When assessing by HIV status, continuation was highest among HIV-negative women (69.4%), moderate among HIV-positive (58.9%) and lowest in studies with unspecified HIV status (48.5%). Stratifying by drug class, ART (58.9%) and unspecified medications (74.0%) were associated with higher continuation, while opioid (23.6%) and antidepressant (28.0%) users had the lowest rates, as reported in . No significant publication bias was detected for the outcome of breastfeeding continuation at 6 months (Egger’s test, p=0.114 and Begg’s test, p=0.844). Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis found a relatively high overall prevalence of breastfeeding initiation (pooled prevalence: 75.2%), while continuation up to 6 months post partum was significantly lower at 53.2%, with both outcomes demonstrating substantial heterogeneity ( I ²=99.2%). Subgroup analyses revealed that breastfeeding prevalence differed by continent, income level, HIV status and drug class. Higher initiation and continuation rates were observed in African and lower-income settings, whereas lower rates were reported in high-income countries and among women using opioids or antidepressants. Meta-regression confirmed that income level and drug class, particularly antidepressant and opioid use, accounted for a significant proportion of the observed heterogeneity ( R ²=49.51% for initiation and R ²=60.77% for continuation). Breastfeeding initiation rates were particularly high among women living with HIV who were receiving ART, with some studies reporting rates exceeding 98%. This trend has been observed in prior studies, where strong public health interventions based on guidelines from national Ministries of Health promoting breastfeeding among women living with HIV and on ART have contributed to high initiation rates, as evidenced by Glaubius et al. For some women, particularly in settings where formula feeding may be less accessible or culturally accepted, breastfeeding may be considered a more practical and affordable option. Also, Levinson et al ’s study described the largest North American cohort of people with HIV who breastfed, most of whom were on ART with undetectable viral loads and experienced no neonatal transmissions. The number of women included in this paper (N=72) reflects that these data were drawn from a time period of the US guideline transition from being prohibitive against breastfeeding in the context of HIV towards a more permissive stance, provided certain conditions relating to adherence and virological suppression were met. Similarly, breastfeeding decisions were influenced by health benefits, community expectations and parent–child bonding. Besides, the study highlights substantial variability in institutional policies, infant prophylaxis and testing practices, as well as the challenges of balancing transmission risks with personal and sociocultural factors. Also, the WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and breastfeeding for up to 2 years regardless of the HIV status; however, the Ugandan guidelines recommend exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and breastfeeding up to 1 year for women living with and on ART. However, McClatchey et al observed that inadequate information regarding medication safety during lactation can lead to uncertainty among healthcare providers in providing recommendations. This uncertainty may result in the premature discontinuation of breastfeeding or the provision of incomplete advice and ambiguous information to the breastfeeding mother. The findings of this study indicate that women using antidepressants and opioids were significantly less likely to continue breastfeeding at 6 months post partum, even after adjusting for potential confounders in multivariable analysis. Several factors may contribute to this association, including concerns about medication transfer to breast milk, maternal well-being and healthcare provider recommendations. Corsi and Murphy and Krans et al revealed that maternal mental health conditions and pain management play a critical role in breastfeeding outcomes. The potential transfer of psychotropic medications such as chlorpromazine and haloperidol through breast milk influences maternal decisions on breastfeeding. Pharmacokinetic and safety data indicate that many antiepileptic drugs, including carbamazepine, valproate, phenytoin, lamotrigine and levetiracetam, have low to moderate transfer into breast milk and are generally compatible with breastfeeding when infants are monitored. However, uncertainty among mothers and healthcare providers can lead to unnecessary discontinuation of treatment or breastfeeding. Continued pharmacokinetic and safety studies, alongside evidence-based counselling, are essential to support safe maternal therapy while promoting breastfeeding. Similarly, a systematic review by Davanzo et al on antidepressants and antipsychotics in lactation showed that drugs do transfer into breastmilk and some can cause infant effects such as jitteriness, respiratory distress and feeding difficulties. As noted by Oystein et al , some healthcare provider recommendations and maternal perceptions of drug safety significantly affect initiation rates in this group. Women taking antidepressants may experience difficulties in breastfeeding due to underlying mental health conditions, such as postpartum depression or anxiety, which can impact motivation, energy levels and self-efficacy in breastfeeding; however, feelings of maternal guilt, disempowerment and trauma around not breastfeeding may have further negative influence on maternal mental health as observed by Hookway et al . Further work to delineate the benefits and risks of breastfeeding while on medication for psychosis and depression is warranted. Similarly, opioid use, whether for chronic pain management or opioid use disorder, has been associated with lower breastfeeding rates. This may be due to maternal sedation, infant withdrawal symptoms or stigma surrounding opioid use in the postpartum period. However, there are clinical situations, such as the use of codeine by mothers with ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolism, where advising against breastfeeding or recommending an alternative medication is appropriate. In such cases, rapid conversion of codeine to morphine can lead to high levels in breast milk, posing a genuine risk to the infant, including reported cases of neonatal death. These polymorphisms occur more frequently, particularly among Ethiopians. Breastfeeding can be beneficial for opioid-exposed infants by reducing the severity of neonatal abstinence syndrome and promoting maternal-infant bonding. Hospital practices, including prenatal education, rooming-in and policies that reduce barriers to breastfeeding, are linked to higher breastfeeding rates as noted by Bogen and Whalen in their review on breastmilk feeding for mothers and infants with opioid exposure. Also, encouraging breastfeeding among women on medication-assisted treatment with buprenorphine or methadone, when clinically appropriate, could improve health outcomes for both mother and child. While methadone and buprenorphine maintenance therapy are compatible with breastfeeding, many women in opioid substance misuse programmes receive inadequate lactation counselling, contributing to lower breastfeeding initiation. Given these findings, healthcare providers must offer clear, evidence-based guidance to women taking antidepressants and opioids, addressing safety concerns while promoting breastfeeding when feasible. Integrating breastfeeding support within perinatal mental health and pain management services could help improve breastfeeding continuation rates in this population. Breastfeeding continuation at 6 months post partum varied widely in this study; individual studies reported significant differences. The highest continuation rate was observed by Yovwin’s study conducted in Nigeria (90.7%), while Welle-strand reported the lowest rate at 21.0%. This variation suggests that multiple factors, such as geographical location, cultural influences, socioeconomic status and healthcare support, play a role in breastfeeding continuation. Importantly, breastfeeding continuation at 6 months declined significantly across all groups. Women using ART had moderate continuation rates, with values ranging from 73.9% to 58.9%. However, women taking antidepressants and antiepileptics experienced a drastic decline. For example, those on antidepressants had a reduction from 86.7% at initiation to 28% at 6 months, while antiepileptic users dropped from 66.3% to 35.8%. A similar trend was observed among opioid users, whose breastfeeding rates fell from 53.5% to 23.6%. The sharp declines among women taking antidepressants, antiepileptics and opioids suggest that medication safety fears, healthcare provider recommendations, maternal health challenges and possible infant-related effects may influence breastfeeding decisions. It is crucial to investigate whether these declines are driven by medical advice, maternal perception of risk, or side effects associated with these medications. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin are generally considered safe in both pregnancy (until 20 weeks of gestation) and lactation, whereas opioids illustrate the complexity of decision-making, with well-documented risks in certain contexts such as codeine use during breastfeeding, alongside other cases where the data are insufficient to draw firm conclusions. Our findings highlight a notable gap between perceived and evidence-based risks of medication use among breastfeeding women. Many mothers overestimate the risks of commonly used drugs, such as psychotropics and opioids, while underestimating the safety of medications like NSAIDs, paracetamol and most antihypertensives. For example, psychotropics and opioids are often perceived as very high risk despite evidence supporting their relative safety when used appropriately, whereas NSAIDs and antihypertensives are generally safe but sometimes viewed as risky. Africa recorded the highest prevalence of breastfeeding at 6 months post partum, with a rate of 66.6%. However, in multivariable analysis, this factor did not demonstrate statistical significance in breastfeeding continuation. The high breastfeeding prevalence in Africa may be attributed to cultural norms, strong community support for breastfeeding and public health initiatives promoting exclusive breastfeeding. Conversely, lower rates in Europe and Asia could reflect work-related constraints or formula-feeding practices in certain regions. The certainty of evidence for both breastfeeding outcomes was limited. According to the GRADE assessment, the evidence for breastfeeding initiation was rated as low certainty, while the evidence for breastfeeding continuation at 6 months was rated as very low certainty. These ratings indicate that the true estimates may differ substantially from the pooled results and therefore should be interpreted with caution. The main reason for downgrading the evidence was the very high heterogeneity across studies ( I ² >90%), suggesting considerable variability in breastfeeding practices among women using medication. Several factors may contribute to this heterogeneity. Differences in country income level, healthcare systems and breastfeeding policies may influence breastfeeding behaviours across settings. Additionally, variation in medication types, maternal health conditions requiring treatment and differences in counselling or guidance provided to women using medications during pregnancy or postpartum may also affect breastfeeding initiation and continuation. Despite conducting subgroup analyses by geography and clinical condition, statistical heterogeneity remained high ( I ²=99.2) for most initiation outcomes. This suggests that the variance may be driven by methodological factors rather than clinical ones. Discrepancies in study design, specifically between retrospective medical record reviews and prospective maternal interviews, as well as variations in study quality and healthcare settings, likely introduced non-sampling errors. Future research using standardised reporting protocols and more homogeneous study designs is required to provide more precise pooled estimates. Also, the high heterogeneity ( I ²=98.1%) observed in most continents indicates substantial within-region variation due to differences in healthcare policies, socioeconomic conditions, maternal education, study populations, healthcare settings, cultural practices and study quality, which limits the generalisability of pooled prevalence estimates. Reflecting the low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted with caution and readers should consider that observed associations and prevalence estimates may change as more robust, prospective data become available. Integrating the GRADE assessment explicitly into the discussion emphasises the need for further high-quality research to strengthen the evidence base and guide clinical and public health recommendations. Also, income status significantly influenced breastfeeding rates; women in high-income countries were less likely to continue breastfeeding at 6 months post partum. This trend is consistent with previous studies, which suggest that various socioeconomic and structural factors influence breastfeeding practices. In high-income settings, early breastfeeding cessation is often attributed to shorter maternity leave policies, increased workforce participation and widespread availability of infant formula. However, this is not always the case. For example, in some regions of England, such as Liverpool, breastfeeding rates are shockingly low even among women who are not employed. This suggests that cultural factors such as the easy availability of formula, limited lactation support and the absence of social networks where breastfeeding is the norm play a significant role in influencing breastfeeding practices. Additionally, cultural beliefs, social norms and convenience-related practices influence maternal decisions. Orkley et al , in predicting breastfeeding rates among primary care trusts, found that in high-income countries, workplace constraints, easy access to formula and a lower perceived need for breastfeeding contribute to reduced prevalence. In contrast, in lower-income settings, breastfeeding is often the primary infant feeding method due to economic constraints and public health promotion efforts. Rates of breastfeeding initiation remain high in low-income countries and among women living with HIV on ART, likely reflecting strong public health efforts. It is important to note that most women living with HIV reside in low- and middle-income countries. Rates of breastfeeding initiation remain high in low-income countries and among women living with HIV on ART, likely reflecting strong public health efforts. It is important to note that most women living with HIV reside in low- and middle-income countries. Until recently, guidelines from high-income countries were quite prohibitive regarding breastfeeding among women with HIV. Although, as indicated by Levison et al , this is starting to change. Nonetheless, these guidelines have become less restrictive; they generally still recommend against breastfeeding. Reflecting on the ‘U=U’ public health campaign, where achieving an undetectable viral load effectively eliminates HIV transmission risk through sexual exposure, there is growing evidence that women on effective ART with sustained viral suppression may safely breastfeed without transmitting HIV to their infants. However, at the time of writing, expert consensus remains that more data are required relating to the rate of breastfeeding HIV transmission among women who have been on long-term suppressive ART before and throughout the recent pregnancy and current breastfeeding. Furthermore, medication use during breastfeeding requires weighing maternal health benefits against potential infant risks. ART exemplifies dual benefit for mother and child, while drugs such as anti-epileptics may protect maternal health but pose infant concerns. This highlights the need for individualised counselling and high-quality safety data to support informed, evidence-based decisions. This may be reflected in the finding that women taking psychotropic medications, opioids and antiepileptics experience significantly lower breastfeeding rates, suggesting that concerns about medication safety and underlying maternal health conditions influence breastfeeding decisions. While in some cases these concerns are supported by evidence, such as known risks with certain opioids like codeine, in many others, the data are limited or reassuring, indicating that perceived risks may outweigh actual evidence of harm. Whereas income status significantly influenced breastfeeding rates in the present analysis, it is important to consider other mediating factors such as maternal education, workplace support and healthcare access. Future research should explore targeted interventions to support breastfeeding continuation across different socioeconomic contexts, particularly in high-income countries where early discontinuation is prevalent. Strengthening maternity leave policies, workplace accommodations for breastfeeding and education on the long-term benefits of breastfeeding may contribute to improved breastfeeding rates globally, as recommended by WHO. Addressing these disparities requires targeted interventions, including healthcare provider training, medication-specific lactation guidelines, medication-specific counselling to breastfeeding women, including guidance on the use of antidepressants, opioids and antiretrovirals, and reinforcing current evidence-based ART recommendations. The challenge is that without the evidence we need, it can be hard to fully weigh up the risks and benefits to each mother and infant and hence the argument for more and higher-quality research is emphasised. Strengthening workplace policies that support breastfeeding, particularly in high-income settings, is also crucial. Furthermore, additional research is needed to explore specific barriers to breastfeeding initiation among women taking various medications and to develop evidence-based interventions that improve breastfeeding support across different populations. Strengths and limitations This study provides critical evidence on the extent and determinants of breastfeeding initiation and continuation among women on medications. The findings demonstrate robustness across analytical approaches and methodologies, supported by a sensitive and comprehensive search strategy. The study highlights the need for targeted interventions to support breastfeeding among high-risk populations, particularly in high-income settings and among women using antidepressants or opioids. The high degree of heterogeneity observed across studies may limit the generalisability of the findings. The presence of publication bias, as evidenced by an asymmetrical funnel plot and confirmed by Egger’s test, suggests a potential under-representation of studies reporting negative or non-significant results. Furthermore, the lack of detailed reporting on key variables, such as HIV status and specific medication types, may introduce residual confounding and impact the accuracy of the estimated effects. Similarly, some studies did not report the study outcome at 6 months post partum. Additionally, the exclusion of grey literature may have introduced publication bias, potentially leading to an overestimation of effects, as studies with non-significant or negative findings are less likely to be published in peer-reviewed journals. There is also a lack of pharmacokinetic data on drug transfer into breast milk for many medications, limiting the ability to fully understand potential risks and benefits to the breastfed infant and, therefore, the ability to provide evidence-based safety guidance. Finally, the reliance on cross-sectional and retrospective study designs further constrains the ability to infer causal relationships between medication use and breastfeeding outcomes. Conclusion Our study highlights that while breastfeeding initiation rates are generally high, significant disparities exist in breastfeeding continuation among women using different medications, influenced by demographic, economic and health-related factors. Introduction and background Did you know that patients with gestational hypertension or preeclampsia have a 3.5 times increased risk of developing chronic hypertension in the future [ ]? Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy account for around 5%-10% of maternal and fetal complications worldwide [ ]. If a hypertensive woman conceives or is known to be taking medications to treat hypertension before pregnancy, this is referred to as chronic hypertension. Gestational hypertension is defined by raised blood pressure (BP) after 20 weeks of gestation without noticeable proteinuria. Similarly, preeclampsia is characterized by an elevation in BP after 20 weeks, accompanied by significant proteinuria or damage to end organs. Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia means a woman with chronic hypertension who develops preeclampsia. These conditions can lead to severe and fatal complications, renal dysfunction, pulmonary edema, seizure, stroke, cardiovascular effects, preterm birth, stillbirth, small for gestational age (SGA), and neonatal asphyxia [ ]. Given these risks, research on preeclampsia prevention is crucial. For example, a recent study demonstrated that aspirin plays a vital role in preventing preeclampsia in high-risk women. However, further research is still needed, as researchers were unable to provide an ideal prophylactic dose of aspirin [ ]. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy continue to present a significant challenge for healthcare providers due to their complex causes, unpredictable course, and long-term effects on both the mother and child [ , ]. This narrative review seeks to influence clinical practice and future research by examining the most relevant and up-to-date data. Furthermore, by identifying gaps in current diagnostic methods, management, and follow-up strategies, this study aims to assist healthcare professionals in implementing interventions to reduce the impact of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. According to reports, the prevalence of hypertension during pregnancy is the leading cause of maternal and infant mortality in the United States. This is noted as one of the risk factors for cardiovascular diseases [ ]. The researchers summarized that the risk of developing chronic hypertension after gestational hypertension and preeclampsia is higher in White women with greater BMI (>35/kg/m 2 ), women with early-onset preeclampsia, and preeclampsia with severe features as compared to normotensive pregnancies [ ]. The chances of developing cardiovascular diseases such as coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, and stroke increase significantly [ ]. The International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy (ISSHP) recommends that ideal management involves regular review of charts and strict BP control, with a target of 110-140/85 mmHg. While mercury sphygmomanometers were historically the gold standard, they are being phased out due to irregular accuracy. Aneroid devices, particularly wall- or trolley-mounted models, are now preferred, with automated monitors under validation for use in pregnancy [ ]. Home BP monitoring (HBPM) is also becoming an essential daily component of care. Postpartum management includes indefinite follow-ups with regular BP monitoring and counseling for a healthy lifestyle and diet [ ]. Proteinuria is a crucial component in the diagnosis of preeclampsia. The 24-hour urine collection method is susceptible to human error. Therefore, spot protein creatinine ratio (PCR) is being facilitated for efficient management. Unfortunately, 24-hour urine tests and spot PCR are not available in most clinical settings, and many physicians have to rely on urine dipstick assessment. However, we should not rely on the urine dipstick test alone. Even if the dipstick test shows protein +2, it is advisable to start treatment for preeclampsia only if the clinical suspicion is positive [ ]. This narrative review aims to critically analyze the advancements from the past 10 years regarding diagnostic tools and methods, introduction, and efficacy of new pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments and highlight the health consequences and outcomes of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in women throughout their reproductive and early middle years. Finally, we will explore how these advancements can lead to better outcomes for the maternal-fetal binomial in the future. This study is a narrative review conducted using the PubMed database. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, a total of 65 articles including randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses on the diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy were included in this review. The inclusion criteria consisted of studies conducted on human adults within the last 10 years and published in English. Discussion Extensive studies have explored the relationship between hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and the increased risk of future cardiovascular complications for both mothers and their children, particularly in terms of prevalence and risk factors. Hypertensive disorders in mothers and fetuses affect approximately 5%-10% of pregnancies and are strongly linked to severe maternal and fetal outcomes. The outcomes include eclampsia, cerebrovascular events, pulmonary edema, severe renal impairment, liver failure, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, and neonatal complications such as fetal or neonatal death, intraventricular hemorrhage, and hyaline membrane disease [ ]. Although there have been significant advancements in the management of these disorders, there remains a gap in understanding how early intervention strategies, such as low-dose aspirin and specific therapies, can further lower BP levels and enhance neonatal and maternal safety. Certain treatments such as labetalol and vitamin E were found to be effective in reducing the BP and protein levels, but further studies are required to evaluate long-term outcomes for both the mother and baby [ ]. Our study aligns with previous study findings, confirming the benefit of combination therapies and low-dose aspirin in regulating hypertensive disorders [ ]. However, we noted differences in long-term cardiovascular outcomes that have not been thoroughly explored in other studies. For instance, our study extends the scope to include long-term cardiovascular health, which may clarify the contrasting results, while other studies focused mainly on short-term maternal and fetal outcomes [ ]. Certain discrepancies may also be attributed to variations in methodology and population characteristics, such as women with a higher pre-pregnancy BMI. Our research highlights the need for long-term cardiovascular health in postpartum women, an aspect that is often overlooked in current studies [ ]. The study also questions prior assumptions regarding the temporary nature of hypertension during pregnancy by demonstrating ongoing target organ damage and increased risk of vascular disorders [ ]. Theoretically, our findings enhance the understanding of hypertensive disorders and their influence on long-term health, particularly in terms of cardiovascular risk. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of continuous postpartum monitoring, emphasizing the necessity for improved follow-up care to manage elevated risks of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular diseases [ ]. An unexpected outcome of our study was the higher prevalence of target organ damage observed within our cohort, suggesting that hypertensive disorders during pregnancy may result in long-term effects on various organ systems. This finding has significant implications for healthcare providers, emphasizing the need for enhanced monitoring and intervention in postpartum to prevent chronic health complications. Additionally, the retrospective design of our study has prevented us from controlling all confounding variables, which may have influenced the results. Future studies should concentrate on large-scale, longitudinal research with more diverse populations to validate our results and assess the long-term effects of hypertensive disorders on maternal cardiovascular health. It would also be beneficial to explore the genetic factors that predispose women to hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and how they influence disease progression and management [ ]. Risk factors for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy include family history of hypertension and diabetes, previous diagnosis of hypertension before pregnancy (the risk of occurrence of gestational hypertension and preeclampsia increased with the presence of elevated BP and stage 1 hypertension) [ ], previous history of preeclampsia in pregnancy, being overweight, unhealthy eating and alcohol consumption [ ], female history of polycystic ovarian syndrome [ ], higher plasmic values of hormone TT3 [ ], and higher sex hormone-binding globulin values (a potential biomarker for pregnancy complications) [ ]. It was also found that specific ophthalmic Doppler parameters are associated with the risk of preeclampsia, as preeclamptic women exhibited differences in three out of six measured values compared to normotensive women. These are time-averaged mean peak velocities (MV), pulsatility index (PI), and end-diastolic velocities (EDVs), which have potential use as predictors of preeclampsia risk [ ]. Prevention Prevention of pregnancy-induced hypertension includes both non-pharmacological and pharmacological approaches. Non-pharmacological strategies involve healthy eating, physical exercise, and control of body weight [ ]. Pharmacologically, metformin use in women diagnosed with gestational diabetes has been shown to reduce the risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension compared to insulin treatment [ ]. Magnesium supplementation, on the other hand, was found to be insufficient in preventing adverse outcomes of pregnancy-induced hypertension by multiple studies [ , ]. However, He et al. found that patients with pregnancy-induced hypertension have lower serum concentrations of zinc, calcium, and magnesium than normotensive pregnant patients [ ]. On the other hand, low-dose aspirin and calcium supplementation were effective in preventing preeclampsia and reducing

Genetics Advancements in genetics have played a significant role in the diagnosis and prevention of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and their adverse outcomes. Hypertension is polygenic, and genetic predisposition to hypertension is a major risk factor for preeclampsia. However, environmental factors, such as BMI, modify the risk of preeclampsia [ ]. The authors state that sequence variants associated with preeclampsia in the maternal genome are ZNF831/20q13 and FTO/16q12, MECOM/3q26, FGF5/4q21, and SH2B3/12q24. Vitamin D receptor gene ApaI and BsmI polymorphisms may also be associated with the susceptibility risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy [ ]. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase gene G894T single-nucleotide polymorphisms were also found to play a significant role in gestational hypertension [ ]. Generally, preeclampsia is associated with elevated levels of TNF and IL-6, cytokines produced primarily by macrophages [ ]. There are also polymorphic variations in fetal genes, transmitted by both the mother and father, which can be linked to the development of hypertension, especially after 20 weeks of pregnancy [ ]. Diagnostic Procedures When it comes to discrepancies regarding the process of diagnosing pregnancy-induced hypertension, a systematic review and meta-analysis stated that there are differences in the diagnosis of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy regarding home and medical office measurement of BP. Home measurements were up to four units smaller for systolic BP and three units smaller for diastolic BP than measurements taken with a health professional, which could affect diagnosis and treatment efficacy [ ]. However, other studies have found different results, indicating that self-BP measurements are effective and similar to office measurements [ ]. Significance of Advancements in Diagnosis Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are defined as systolic BP ≥ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg during pregnancy [ ]. Therefore, the diagnosis is made through accurate BP measurement. HBPM has been proven as a reliable and straightforward method for measuring an individual's BP, offering better reproducibility than 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM). HBPM is user-friendly, easy to learn, and does not require visits to a doctor or a hospital, making it accessible and cost-effective. Additionally, it can help differentiate between white coat and masked hypertension [ ]. Similarly, a study by Tran et al. concluded that HBPM is particularly useful for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, offering benefits such as fewer antenatal visits and timely medication adjustments [ ]. However, its broader implementation is limited by a lack of sufficient evidence. Future studies should focus on using validated devices, collecting reference data from healthy pregnant women, and establishing clear diagnostic and treatment guidelines [ ]. Preeclampsia is defined by gestational hypertension associated with protein in the urine. Proteinuria is confirmed if urinary protein excretion is ≥300 mg over 24 hours in a urine sample or ≥1+ on qualitative dipstick examination. Alternatively, it could be a protein-to-creatinine ratio ≥ 30 mg/mmol or ≥0.3 mg/dL [ ]. However, further diagnostic and prognostic tools are currently under research. A study by Chen et al. highlighted the potential for simultaneous fetal aneuploidy screening and prediction of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy using second-trimester blood samples to measure alpha-fetoprotein, free β-hCG, and D-dimer levels [ ]. D-dimer alone was also an effective predictive marker for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. The combination of D-dimer, alpha-fetoprotein, and free beta-hCG demonstrated higher screening efficiency than the traditional alpha-fetoprotein and free β-hCG model, with a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) > 0.800 for severe preeclampsia, preeclampsia, and gestational hypertension. This research demonstrated clinical significance in identifying women at risk for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, improving screening sensitivity, and supporting early intervention strategies. Expanding the use of these innovative prenatal screening approaches could enhance maternal care, particularly for high-risk pregnancies [ ]. Additionally, regarding preeclampsia markers, soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) levels can increase by 5-6 times and strongly correlate with the disease's incidence. In contrast, placental growth factor (PLGF) levels gradually increase during pregnancy, showing high sensitivity and specificity in predicting preeclampsia. The sFlt-1/PLGF ratio can serve as a key biomarker for both early-onset (20-33 + 6 weeks) and late-onset (>34 weeks) preeclampsia, with ratios exceeding 85 and 110, respectively, indicating a high-risk pregnancy [ ]. Treatment When it comes to the treatment of hypertension in pregnancy, NICE guidelines stipulate that the commencement of antihypertensive treatment after birth should happen at 150/100 mmHg. Attar et al. evaluated the possible effects of pharmacological management on both maternal and fetal outcomes of patients with mild-to-moderate hypertension during pregnancy and concluded that antihypertensive treatments resulted in a lower risk of maternal outcomes, including severe hypertension [ ]. Findings from the Control of Hypertension in Pregnancy Study (CHIPs) trial by Magee et. al are similar to the above finding [ ]. The CHIPs was a multicentric trial that investigated whether a tight (target diastolic BP of 85 mmHg) or less tight (target diastolic BP of 100 mmHg) BP control could yield a long-term outcome. At the end of the study, they concluded that treatment of mild hypertension led to better outcomes. However, this result cannot be relied upon as the main objective of the CHIPs trial was to compare whether less tight BP or tight BP control could yield better outcomes and most of the participants were already on antihypertensive medications, and no comparison was made between patients who had started antihypertensive and those just starting; therefore, conclusions could not be made on the advantages and disadvantages of less tight and tight BP controls. Initially, in 2015, the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) disputed lowering the BP to 140/90 mmHg. But, in 2022, they supported the target BP of 140/90 mmHg in patients with hypertension, as it is more beneficial in reducing the risk of long-term maternal complications [ , ]. Medical Management Most women who experience high BP during pregnancy have a significantly increased likelihood of developing long-term hypertension. However, there is an inconsistency in the management of high BP postpartum [ ]. Different recommendations have been made, but the medication preference has not been stated due to a lack of sufficient data [ ]. Mostly, the medication choice is dependent on the regimen used during the antepartum period, but the optimal treatment strategy remains unclear due to limited studies [ ]. Recently, the predominantly prescribed antihypertensive medications in pregnancy are labetalol, methyldopa, and nifedipine [ ]. However, there is no conclusive evidence on the most commonly used medicines during this period [ ]. A review by Cairns et al. found some evidence showing that calcium channel blockers, vasodilators, and beta-blockers reduce BP postpartum [ ]. However, there was no conclusion on which group of drugs was more efficient [ ]. Alavifard et al. compared hydralazine, nifedipine, and labetalol as initial treatment for severely high BP in pregnant women and found no significant difference in the cesarean section rates or maternal side effects [ ]. However, nifedipine showed a marginal advantage [ ]. Hup et al. argued that nifedipine is preferred due to its dosing rate of 1-2 times a day, compared to labetalol, which is given three times a day [ ]. It should also be considered that nifedipine has been shown to have more side effects than labetalol [ ]. A recent study by Irfan et al. concluded that most antihypertensive medications are effective; therefore, this lack of restriction allows prescriptions to be tailored to patients' individual needs [ ]. Non-medical Management Wen and Liu examined the effects of information-knowledge-attitude-practice (IKAP) and health education combined with cluster-based care in patients with gestational hypertension [ ]. Their focus was on providing individual and group health information by distributing health education manuals to hypertensive patients during pregnancy and also to their families. Their study showed that the combination of IKAP and cluster care had a significant difference in preventing maternal outcomes as compared to cluster care alone, with results of more adequate weight and BP regulation, a smaller incidence of negative pregnancy and neonatal outcomes (including placenta previa, cesarean deliveries, unhealthy amounts of amniotic fluid, fetal suffering, and postpartum bleeding), and better postpartum recovery and general life quality (including increased physical exercise, better emotional and mental health, reduced pain and discomfort, and better sleep) [ ]. The aim of the treatment of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy is to reduce maternal risks, including cerebrovascular injuries, cardiovascular stress, and renal trauma, and to mitigate fetal risks due to ongoing adverse effects of the antihypertensive medications, which causes a reduction in uteroplacental perfusion [ ]. This is of utmost importance, as the aim outlines a dual-protection approach for the mother and the fetus. The initial plan of action begins with adequate prenatal care, timely diagnosis, and efficient delivery of the newborn [ ], indicating that prompt diagnosis, regular BP surveillance, and target BP control lead to reduced prenatal risk and severe maternal hypertension. However, cases of preeclampsia prompt caution due to the severity of complications, including hypertension, seizures, and intracerebral hemorrhage [ ]. According to research, it is best to prolong pregnancy when the mother is <34 weeks; however, in situations where the maternal risk increases with the prolonged pregnancy, it is advisable to take the necessary steps to deliver the fetus. During delivery, corticosteroids are used to promote lung maturity in the fetus. Women may also receive magnesium sulfate, which is associated with a reduced risk of maternal death and fetal benefits [ ]. Impact of Advancements on Prognosis and Long-Term Outcomes Significant advancements have been made in the topic of prognosis and long-term management of hypertension during pregnancy. The implementation of pharmacological interventions has notably influenced the prognosis of hypertensive disorders, positively impacting maternal and fetal outcomes. A meta-analysis investigating the administration of antihypertensive medications for mild-to-moderate hypertension in pregnancy demonstrated a marked reduction in the incidence of severe hypertension, preeclampsia, and placental abruption. It did not contribute to adverse long-term outcomes such as SGA infants or fetal mortality [ ]. Early detection and proactive management of hypertension are pivotal to improving long-term prognosis. Additionally, another meta-analysis included several randomized controlled trials that revealed that the combination of low-dose aspirin and calcium supplementation significantly mitigated the long-term risks of preterm birth and postpartum hemorrhage by preventing preeclampsia [ ]. These findings highlight the vital role of early detection and timely intervention in the prevention of hypertension and preeclampsia. This is just an example [ ]. Limitations of the study The comprehensive nature of the literature review, along with the inclusion of published evidence-based studies, is the strength of this review. Our review was limited by the English language and US population and included articles within the past 10 years. Another limitation is the discretion in choosing the articles that helped extend our knowledge about this topic, leading to selection bias. There are multiple barriers to monitoring the prevalence of hypertension in pregnancy. The use of various EMR systems with a slightly different definition of hypertension can lead to information bias. Another limitation is the short duration of outcomes, as some clinical trials are still ongoing. Some studies collected data from participants at home using BP monitors that differed from those used in other studies. There could also be financial constraints for some studies, which can lead to a lower recruitment rate and funding bias. The sample size can also lead to bias, as a smaller sample size results in less statistical power. Various studies were used in this review, and most of them had their own design. Each clinical trial has its own set of inclusion and exclusion criteria, which can lead to data discrepancies. Summary Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy complicate approximately 5%-10% of pregnancies and are directly associated with adverse outcomes for both the fetus and the mother [ ]. Maternal complications include eclampsia, cerebrovascular events, and placental abruption, while perinatal complications include fetal or neonatal death [ ]. Recent advancements in treatment include combination therapy with labetalol, low-dose aspirin, vitamin E, and calcium, which significantly lowered BP and 24-hour proteinuria levels [ ]. Another study concluded that oral nifedipine was superior to IV labetalol and IV hydralazine for treating severe hypertension in pregnancy [ ]. However, further network meta-analyses are needed to compare drugs within the same class, dosage variations, and administration timing to determine the most effective regimen for preventing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy [ ]. The use of aspirin as the first-line treatment for preeclampsia prevention is supported by the need for anticoagulant therapy to treat maternal coagulation dysfunction. Its effectiveness alone is limited, particularly in high-risk cases. Therefore, the World Health Organization recommends calcium supplementation, especially for pregnant women with low calcium levels or inadequate dietary intake. Although further research is needed, studies suggest that combining low-dose aspirin with calcium supplementation may reduce the incidence of preeclampsia and improve maternal and fetal outcomes [ ]. Regarding delivery timing, the When to Induce Labour to Limit Risk in Pregnancy Hypertension (WILL) randomized trial findings support planned birth at 38 + 0-3 weeks as a safe clinical option, with no significant differences in adverse maternal or neonatal outcomes [ ]. After childbirth, women who had hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are at a 3.5 times higher risk of developing chronic hypertension and have a 1.7-2.8 times greater risk of cardiovascular disease compared to those without such conditions [ ]. These patients might present target organ damage across multiple systems, such as cardiac and renal, persisting to some extent for up to four decades postpartum. The high prevalence highlights the need for further research into disease progression and risk assessment, as well as exploring interventions to improve clinical outcomes [ ]. Additionally, following hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, adequate postpartum care is needed, which includes regular BP monitoring, physical activity, smoke cessation, a balanced diet, and weight management to support long-term cardiovascular health [ ]. Considering the complexity of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, this review aims to critically analyze how recent medical research influences the diagnosis and management of these conditions. We seek to raise awareness of potential long-term complications, improve clinical outcomes, and identify knowledge gaps that could guide future research. Conclusions After the critical analysis of several works of literature, we were able to find compelling evidence that the risk factors include a family history of hypertension, diabetes, and a previous history of preeclampsia in pregnancy. High plasma values of the hormone TT3 and sex hormone-binding globulin were found to be potential biomarkers for detecting pregnancy complications. As far as diagnosis, spot PCR is effective in early detection and management, but its availability in most clinical settings is limited. Regular BP monitoring and daily HBPM are found to be effective. Regarding the therapeutic approach, a combination of low-dose aspirin, labetalol, vitamin E, and calcium seems to lower BP. Oral nifedipine helps in treating severe hypertension, while calcium helps in preventing gestational hypertension in nulliparous/primigravida women. Aspirin is given prophylactically for chronic hypertension. A target BP of 140/90 mmHg is more beneficial in reducing the risk of long-term maternal complications. Treatment of mild hypertension leads to better outcomes. Aerobic and resistance exercises were found to be effective. Planned birth at 38 weeks significantly improved maternal and fetal outcomes. Postpartum follow-ups are needed for regular BP monitoring along with counseling for a healthy lifestyle and diet to reduce long-term complications. However, larger studies are needed to confirm these findings and their underlying mechanisms. Hence, we conclude that there is an urgent need to create awareness between healthcare providers and expectant mothers to help with early detection, appropriate management, and prevention of hypertensive disorders. Despite progress in diagnosing and managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, they still manage to be a significant concern for both mother and fetal health worldwide, suggesting further research on understanding their development, genetic involvement, screening techniques, novel therapeutic approaches, and long-term implications to have better consequences for both mothers and their infants.

Introduction Medication use during pregnancy and breastfeeding is common, with an estimated 80%‐90% of women reporting the use of at least one (prescribed) medicine during pregnancy [ ]. Nonprescription or over-the-counter (OTC) medicines are frequently used to manage pregnancy-related or seasonal symptoms such as heartburn, pain, or cold symptoms [ ]. Although readily available in supermarkets and drugstores, OTC medicines are not without risk. Inappropriate use of some OTC medicines may increase the risk of congenital anomalies, adverse perinatal outcomes, and long-term health consequences for the offspring [ ]. For instance, use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen or naproxen in the second half of pregnancy has been associated with higher risks of constriction of the ductus arteriosus, oligohydramnios, and fetal renal dysfunction [ ]. Similarly, the use of certain antihistamines during breastfeeding may reduce milk supply or cause sedation and irritability in infants, especially at high doses or with prolonged use [ ]. While some women may be unaware of these potential risks, others tend to overestimate teratogenic risks and may be reluctant to use necessary medications to manage health conditions (eg, fever or pain during pregnancy), which in some cases could result in greater harm than the medications themselves [ ]. Empowering women to make informed medication choices is therefore essential. Compared with prescription medicines, OTC medicines are widely available, less stringently regulated, and frequently used without professional guidance [ ]. This shifts the responsibility for safety assessment to the individual user. Uninformed decisions about taking OTC medicines (including herbs, homeopathic remedies, and supplements) may lead to the usage of unsafe medicines without the user even being aware. While teratogenic risk information is available online, it has been suggested to be unclear, hard to find, or challenging to interpret for the lay audience. Hence, new interventions tailored to the target population are needed. Electronic health (eHealth) apps are described as the next generation in prenatal care and have been demonstrated to improve antenatal care quality, medication adherence, and pregnancy outcomes [ ]. Research suggests that up to 95% of pregnant women search online for health information [ ]. Mobile apps have become one of the primary sources of information and tend to rapidly replace traditional methods of obtaining information from health professionals and written resources [ ]. Consequently, there are more apps available with pregnancy-related information compared to any other medical topic at the time of this writing [ ]. While online information is easily accessible for women of reproductive age, it also entails risks, particularly regarding the reliability and accuracy of online sources [ ]. Conflicting information from multiple online sources is common and can result in women seeking additional unreliable sources, experiencing increased anxiety or even avoiding necessary medication [ ]. For example, previous research suggests that the main reasons women are hesitant to take medication during lactation include fear of harming the infant, lack of clear and consistent information, and conflicting advice (eg, between health care providers and the often outdated and overly restrictive information provided in the product label) [ ]. This can lead women to discontinue breastfeeding or avoid necessary medication, even though most medications are compatible with breastfeeding [ ]. Therefore, it is important to develop a single tool that is integrated across all stages of maternity care, providing reliable, clear, and comprehensible safety information. Although several apps providing medication safety information for pregnancy or breastfeeding have been developed, awareness and use of these tools remain suboptimal, as they are often not easily accessible or widely known to users [ ]. In addition, since brands of OTC medicines, use patterns, and regulatory recommendations on safety during pregnancy and lactation differ between countries, each country bears responsibility for providing, maintaining, and effectively disseminating locally relevant recommendations on medication safety [ ]. In response to these challenges, this study aims to describe the development and dissemination process of a free and easily accessible Dutch mobile app on the safety of OTC medicines during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Methods Overview The app is developed by the Dutch Teratology Information Service (TIS), part of Pharmacovigilance Centre Lareb. The Dutch TIS is the national knowledge center for medication safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding [ ]. TIS provides evidence-based information on over 1100 (primarily prescription) drugs through a knowledge bank on its public website, which receives approximately 1.5 million visits annually [ ]. Next to the knowledge bank, there was a desire for easier and faster access to information on OTC medications, for example, when standing in the drugstore. The 2-year development and implementation project started on May 1, 2023. This study followed a development and formative evaluation approach in which data were collected through questionnaires and focus groups to iteratively refine the new mobile app. This study followed 5 consecutive phases, including preparation, development, preimplementation, implementation, and evaluation ( ). The month numbers displayed in Figure 1 represent the month of the year. Phase 1. Preparation Phase First, a project group consisting of representatives from the professional associations of midwives and gynecologists, as well as a delegate from the umbrella organizations representing drugstores, was assembled. Next, a needs assessment was conducted among the target population using 2 tailored online questionnaires, one for women who were pregnant or gave birth within the past year and one for health care professionals working with this group. These were the only inclusion criteria for participating in the needs assessment. Questions focused on information-seeking behavior, content preferences, and distribution strategies. Given their brief and exploratory nature, the questionnaires primarily assessed opinions and prior behaviors and were therefore not pilot-tested nor formally validated. A translated version of one of the distributed questionnaires is provided as supplemental material. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling approaches, primarily through the Dutch Pregnancy Drug Registry (as part of the Dutch TIS), social media, an umbrella organization of drugstores, and the TIS’s professional network. Together, these recruitment strategies aimed to provide a comprehensive representation of the target population, thereby reducing the risk of sampling bias. The target sample size of 100 completed questionnaires was determined based on feasibility considerations and the exploratory aims of the study. The completed questionnaires were analyzed descriptively and extensively discussed within the project group, and the outcomes were used as a basis for the development phase. Phase 2. Development Phase During the development phase, an initial draft of the app was devised together with a marketing agency and information technology partner. When developing the app prototype, insights from the needs assessment were used, and discussions with the project group addressed which barriers health care professionals needed to overcome before recommending the app. Key decisions included the navigation structure, type of information, required warnings, interface design, app name, and integration with the existing TIS knowledge bank on the website for extended content. A comprehensive list of OTC medicines, such as analgesics, antacids, vitamins, and herbal supplements, was based on the most commonly used OTC medicines during pregnancy in the Dutch Pregnancy Drug Registry and further extended with OTC medicines identified during field visits to pharmacies, drugstores, and supermarkets. Medicine safety information included in the app was drafted by teratology experts from the Dutch TIS, based on the latest scientific available evidence. Content drafting was supervised by a medical doctor and a pharmacist. All displayed content was fully managed in-house, allowing for continuous updates and modifications as needed. Finally, in consultation with legal experts, privacy terms and disclaimers were carefully drafted. By the end of this phase, a fully functional app prototype was completed. Phase 3. Preimplementation Phase Before the launch, a prototype of the app was extensively tested among the target population using a mixed method approach by collecting both qualitative data (focus groups) and quantitative data (questionnaires). First, focus groups were conducted consisting of target users and teratology experts. Participants were recruited through convenience and snowball-based approaches, primarily via midwifery practices, pregnancy fitness classes, and professional networks. Each focus group was scheduled for a maximum of one hour. Participants first completed exercises designed to facilitate navigation through the app, after which the facilitator led a group discussion following a predesigned script, eliciting feedback aimed at improving the app. Sessions were audio-recorded with consent, and all feedback points were documented and descriptively analyzed without the use of an analytical framework. We aimed to conduct 5 focus groups with a minimum of 5 participants each, a target determined pragmatically in light of feasibility and the short data collection timeframe. Subsequently, an online questionnaire, mirroring the focus group tasks, was distributed among health care providers and women who were pregnant or gave birth within the past year. These were the only inclusion criteria for administering the questionnaire.

Health care professionals were positioned as key figures by recommending the app during consultations, as part of a motivational approach. Booster campaigns were periodically initiated to reach the continuously changing target population. All feedback received from app users was carefully reviewed, and whenever possible, immediate additions or changes were made to the content. Phase 5. Evaluation Phase Evaluation metrics included the number of app downloads, App Store ratings, user feedback, number of daily active users, most searched medications, and total number of page views. Tracking of anonymous in-app user behavior commenced 5 months postlaunch, following an app release. Ethical Considerations This study did not require approval from a medical ethics review committee, as it did not qualify as medical research involving human subjects under the Dutch Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act. All collected data were anonymized before analysis to protect participant privacy and confidentiality. Participation was voluntary, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation. Only focus group participants received a gift voucher of their choice as a token of appreciation for their time and contribution. Results Phase 1. Preparation Phase A total of 217 individuals completed the needs assessment questionnaire; 184 (84.8%) were women who were pregnant or had given birth within the past year, and 33 (15.2%) were health care professionals ( ). Among the women, 160 out of 184 (87.0%) were pregnant at the moment of administering the questionnaire (mainly in the second trimester), and 10 out of the 24 women who recently gave birth (41.7%) were still breastfeeding. The majority of women (134/184, 72.8%) reported actively seeking safety information before using any medication. The need for information on OTC medicines (142/184, 77.2%) and health products (eg, supplements, herbs, and vitamins; 122/184, 66.3%) was higher than the need for information on prescribed medicines (70/184, 38.0%). Preferred sources of information were official (government) websites (151/184, 82.1%), product information (125/184, 67.9%), and health care providers (115/184, 62.5%). The primary motivation for seeking safety information was (1) to determine whether a medicine can be used during pregnancy and breastfeeding or not (2), which medicine is the preferred treatment option for specific (pregnancy) complaints, and (3) what the possible adverse drug reactions are. Open-ended responses underscored challenges in finding trustworthy and accessible information, and frustration with inconsistent recommendations across sources. Health care professionals (n=33) reported using the knowledge bank of TIS on the website frequently and appreciated the clear distinction between pregnancy and breastfeeding guidance. The main reasons for seeking safety information were (1) to determine whether or not a medicine can be used during pregnancy and breastfeeding (2), what the possible adverse drug reactions are, and (3) which medicine is the preferred treatment option for specific (pregnancy) complaints. While some believed the app could reduce their workload, others expected women would still seek personal advice. Finally, health care professionals were moderately likely to use the app themselves (mean 6.0, SD 3.5) but more likely to recommend it to patients (mean 7.3, SD 2.4 out of a scale from 1 to 10).
